description.en: Students conduct a treasure hunt (outdoors if possible, indoors if not) to find natural or "found" objects. They sort their findings into categories, create simple value cards describing why each item matters, and display them in a class "treasure gallery."
description.es: Students conduct a treasure hunt (outdoors if possible, indoors if not) to find natural or "found" objects. They sort their findings into categories, create simple value cards describing why each item matters, and display them in a class "treasure gallery."

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Small paper bag or envelope for each student (recycled/brought from home, or classroom supply)

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: Ask: "What did Layla and her friends find in the garden? Did they pay for any of it?" Establish the question: can you find something valuable today that costs nothing?

steps.title: Treasure Walk (5 min)
steps.description: Students walk around the classroom (or school hallway/outdoor space) and collect 2-3 "treasures" — anything interesting they notice. Indoors: a pretty eraser, a leaf that blew in, an interesting paper shape. Outdoors: rocks, leaves, sticks, pinecones.

steps.title: Share & Sort (2 min)
steps.description: Back at desks, each student holds up their favorite find. Quick class sort: "Is it pretty? Useful? Interesting?" Teacher tallies on board.

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "Did any of these cost money? What makes them worth keeping?"

discussionQuestions: What did you find that surprised you?
Why is your favorite treasure valuable to you?
Would you trade it for a dollar? Why or why not?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Small paper bag for each student
Index cards or half-sheets of scrap paper (3 per student)
Outdoor space or classroom "hunt zones" set up in advance

steps.title: Introduction & Rules (3 min)
steps.description: Review story. Set hunt rules: find 3 things you didn't buy and would want to keep. No living plants. No one else's belongings. Indoors: use "found" items in designated zones (teacher pre-places interesting objects around the room).

steps.title: Treasure Hunt (8 min)
steps.description: Students search and collect their 3 items.

steps.title: Create Value Cards (5 min)
steps.description: For each item, complete a value card: "I found a ___. It's special because ___. It would cost money to buy because ___. But I got it for ___ (free / found it)."

steps.title: Gallery Share (3 min)
steps.description: Students lay their items and value cards on their desks. Quick gallery walk.

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "What made the best treasure? Was it the rarest? The prettiest? The most useful?"

discussionQuestions: Could you sell any of these? How much would you charge?
What's something FREE in our neighborhood that people might not notice?
Is something free worth less than something you buy? Why or why not?
What did Layla's friends have that the garden GAVE them?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Small paper bags for each student
Index cards for value cards (3 per student)
Tape or sticky tack to display cards alongside items
Large paper or whiteboard section for class "free resource" brainstorm

steps.title: Introduction & Planning (3 min)
steps.description: Review story. Pose: "You're setting up a Treasure Exhibition like the friends did at the end of Season 1. Your exhibition only has items that cost $0. What will you display?"

steps.title: Hunt (10 min)
steps.description: Students collect 3-5 items.

steps.title: Value Cards — Detailed (10 min)
steps.description: Each card: name, where found, why valuable, estimated "store price" if someone sold it, and why you'd display it in your exhibition.

steps.title: Exhibition Setup (5 min)
steps.description: Each student arranges their items on their desk with value cards displayed.

steps.title: Gallery Walk (5 min)
steps.description: Students walk the room, place a star sticker (or make a check mark) next to the item they find most valuable. They may not choose their own.

steps.title: Data & Reflection (2 min)
steps.description: Count stars. Which item got the most? Discuss: "Did the most popular item cost money? What made it win?"

discussionQuestions: How is the value of a found rock different from the value of a rock you'd buy at a store?
What makes something a 'treasure' vs. just a random object?
Layla found a smooth stone. What made it valuable to her — and not necessarily to someone else?
Is there such a thing as a free resource that costs something? (Like a park — who pays for it?)
Name three free resources in our school or neighborhood that people overlook.
extensionIdeas: Start a class "nature collection" that grows over weeks — add one found item per student per week
Take photos of found treasures and create a digital class museum
Research: what did kids in another era (1800s, 1900s) use as toys and treasures? Compare to today

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: Classroom supplies and found/donated materials
items: Paper bags (recycled, from home, or folded from newspaper)
Scrap paper for value cards
Pencils or crayons (classroom supply)
Teacher pre-places interesting objects around room for indoor hunt (pencil toppers, interesting erasers, leaves, etc.)

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
items: Index cards for value cards (~$3/100 pack ÷ 25 students = $0.12/student, reusable)
Star stickers for gallery walk voting (~$2/sheet ÷ class = negligible)
Colored pencils (shared set)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Small cloth or paper drawstring bag for each student to store their treasures (~$1-2/student)
Cardstock value cards (sturdier, students keep)
Printed "Treasure Hunter" certificate for each student

focus: Find and name 2–3 natural objects with a partner
Sort finds into simple groups: rocks, sticks, leaves
Draw a favorite find instead of writing
Words: treasure, find, sort
Find and sort 4–5 objects on your own
Make a value card with a frame: "This ___ matters because ___"
Tell why one item is special to you
Vocabulary: collect, category, value
Choose your own categories and explain them
Compare two finds on a value card
Set up a labeled gallery display
Vocabulary: criteria, compare, curate
Build a classification system and defend your categories
Weigh usefulness against sentiment on each value card
Curate the gallery with a written rationale
Vocabulary: classification, rationale, intrinsic value

description.en: Students plant a seed (or simulate planting with a paper "seed" in a cup) and simultaneously start a "savings journal" that tracks a parallel question: if you save $1 every week, how much do you have in 4 weeks? 8 weeks? 1 year? Both timelines run side by side — the seed and the savings jar grow together.
description.es: Students plant a seed (or simulate planting with a paper "seed" in a cup) and simultaneously start a "savings journal" that tracks a parallel question: if you save $1 every week, how much do you have in 4 weeks? 8 weeks? 1 year? Both timelines run side by side — the seed and the savings jar grow together.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: One index card or half-sheet of paper per student

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: Ask: "How long did Frances say it would take for a seed to grow?" (1-2 weeks.) "What if you put $1 in a jar every week — how long until you have $10?" Establish the parallel: seeds and savings both need time.

steps.title: Draw Your Savings Jar (4 min)
steps.description: Students draw a large jar on their paper. Inside, they draw 10 sections (coins or lines) representing 10 weeks of saving $1. Color in Week 1.

steps.title: Prediction (2 min)
steps.description: Students write or say: "By Week 4 I will have $___. By Week 10 I will have $___."

steps.title: Discussion (2 min)
steps.description: "What's the hardest part of saving — getting the first dollar, or not spending it while you wait?"

discussionQuestions: Why was it hard for Riley to wait for her seed to grow?
Have you ever saved up for something? How long did it take?
What's the difference between spending money and saving it?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Small plastic or paper cup per student (recycled deli cups work)
Potting soil (shared bag) or shredded paper to simulate soil
One fast-germinating seed per student (radish or bean, OR use a dried bean as "seed" with no expectation of planting)
"Savings Journal" worksheet (hand-drawn on paper: jar outline + 8-week tracker grid)

steps.title: Savings Journal Setup (5 min)
steps.description: Students draw their savings jar tracker: a jar with 8 rows labeled Week 1 through Week 8. Each row = $1 saved. "By Week 8, you'd have $8 — what could you buy with $8?"

steps.title: Plant Your Seed (7 min)
steps.description: Fill cups with soil. Make a small hole. Place seed. Cover gently. Label with name marker. Water lightly.

steps.title: Parallel Predictions (5 min)
steps.description: Students complete two predictions: "I think my seed will sprout in ___ days" and "If I save $1 per week for 8 weeks, I'll have ___. I could use that to buy ___."

steps.title: Week 1 Entry (2 min)
steps.description: Color in Week 1 on their savings jar. Date it.

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "What do both your seed and your savings jar need? (Time and not messing with it.)"

discussionQuestions: Riley wanted to check her seed every hour. What happens if you spend your savings every week instead of letting it grow?
Frances said seeds make more seeds. What happens to savings if you add to it every week?
Is waiting easier when you can see what's growing? What if you can't see it yet?
What's one thing you could save for that would take 8 weeks?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Folded mini-book (2 pieces of paper folded in half = 8 pages)
Printed or hand-drawn "savings growth chart" (weekly amounts for $1/week over 52 weeks)

steps.title: Plant Your Seed (8 min)
steps.description: Follow same planting steps as 30-minute version. This time, students also set up a "seed observation log" page in their mini-book — date, appearance of soil, drawing of cup.

steps.title: Build Your Savings Portfolio (12 min)
steps.description: Students create a 4-page savings section in their mini-book: Page 1: "My Savings Goal" (what they're saving for, cost, how long at $1/week) Page 2: A hand-drawn growth chart (weeks 1-12 filled in, rest blank) Page 3: "What could I skip buying this week to save $1?" (list of small purchases they make or see family make) Page 4: "What will I have after 1 year if I save $1/week?" (calculate: $52)

steps.title: Seed vs. Savings Comparison (8 min)
steps.description: Pair discussion: "Your seed will become a plant in 2 weeks. Your savings will become your goal in ___ weeks. What's the same about both processes?" Partners report one similarity to the class.

steps.title: Class Savings Jar (5 min)
steps.description: On a large piece of paper displayed in class, everyone adds their name and their savings goal. Will check in monthly.

steps.title: Reflection (2 min)
steps.description: "Frances has been saving seeds for years. What would a person's savings look like if they saved $1/week for 10 years?" (Answer: $520.)

discussionQuestions: Frances said: 'You start with something small. You wait patiently. Then you get something big.' How is this true for both seeds and savings?
If you check your savings every day, does it grow faster? What about if you add $2/week instead of $1?
What's the hardest thing about not spending money you have?
Benny chose sunflower seeds — the biggest kind. If you want to save MORE, what do you change?
What's one thing your family already grows, makes, or saves instead of buying?
extensionIdeas: Weekly seed observation logs maintained for the full growth cycle (photograph or draw)
Create a class savings chart on the wall that fills in each week for 8 weeks
Research: what does a savings account do with your money while you wait? (Interest — brief intro for T4)

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: No planting — full simulation with paper
items: Paper cup (students bring one from home or use recycled)
Scrap paper for savings journal (folded into mini-book)
Pencils/crayons (classroom supply)
Teacher draws the savings jar template on the board; students copy

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
items: Potting soil (1 small bag ~$4 ÷ 25 students = $0.16/student)
Bean or radish seeds (~$2/packet for 30 seeds = $0.07/student)
Craft sticks for plant labels (~$2/50 pack = $0.04/student)
Printed savings journal worksheet (shared printer cost)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Small terra cotta pot per student (~$0.50-1/student, students take home)
Pre-printed, illustrated savings journal mini-book (~$0.50/student)
Seed packet selection (3-4 varieties, students choose) (~$0.50/student)
"My Growing Plan" cardstock cover for mini-book

focus: Plant a seed and check on it with the teacher
Add one coin to the jar each week
Draw the plant as it grows
Words: grow, save, wait, more
Track growth and savings on a simple chart
Predict next week's total with a sentence frame
Notice that small amounts add up over time
Vocabulary: savings, weekly, patience, total
Calculate savings over 4 and 8 weeks
Graph plant growth alongside money growth
Explain how waiting leads to a bigger result
Vocabulary: estimate, growth, compare, goal
Project savings over a year and explain the pattern
Model how consistent saving builds up
Argue why patience pays off using your data
Vocabulary: compounding, projection, long-term, return

description.en: Students bring 1-3 small items from home (pencils, stickers, small toys, trading cards, books) and set up a classroom trading post. Before trading, each student creates "value cards" for their items. They then trade using only negotiation — no play money, just agreement. The goal: end up with something you value more than what you started with.
description.es: Students bring 1-3 small items from home (pencils, stickers, small toys, trading cards, books) and set up a classroom trading post. Before trading, each student creates "value cards" for their items. They then trade using only negotiation — no play money, just agreement. The goal: end up with something you value more than what you started with.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 1 small item per student (brought from home — pencil, eraser, small toy, sticker sheet, trading card)

steps.title: Trade Rules (2 min)
steps.description: Review: both people must agree. You can say no. A trade is fair if both people feel happy after. Demonstrate: teacher and student model a trade. "I'll trade you this red pencil for that eraser — deal?"

steps.title: Round 1 (3 min)
steps.description: Turn to partner on right. Make one trade offer. Both can accept or decline. If you both agree, swap. If not, each keeps their item.

steps.title: Round 2 (3 min)
steps.description: Rotate 2 seats. New partner. New trade opportunity. "Can I offer you my ___ for your ___?"

steps.title: Round 3 & Debrief (2 min)
steps.description: One final rotation. After: "Raise your hand if you ended up with something you like better than what you started with."

discussionQuestions: Did you trade? Why or why not?
Did anyone say no to a trade? Was that okay?
What made a trade feel fair?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 2-3 small items per student (brought from home)
Index cards or half-sheets of paper (3 per student for value cards)

steps.title: Create Value Cards (6 min)
steps.description: For each item, students make a value card: draw the item, write or dictate "This is a ___. I'd trade it for ___ because ___." The card helps others know what the student wants in exchange.

steps.title: Set Up Trading Stations (2 min)
steps.description: Each student arranges their items on their desk with value cards propped up or laid out — their "trading booth."

steps.title: Gallery Walk (3 min)
steps.description: Students walk around and look at all items. They may NOT trade yet — just browse. Mental notes only.

steps.title: Open Trading (7 min)
steps.description: Free-form trading period. Students approach each other with specific offers: "I'll trade you my ___ for your ___ — deal?" Both must agree.

steps.title: Reflection Circle (2 min)
steps.description: Sit in circle. Share: "I traded my ___ for ___ because ___." Anyone who didn't trade says why they chose to keep their item.

discussionQuestions: Was there something lots of people wanted? What happened to its 'trade value'?
Did everyone agree on what was worth trading for? Why not?
How is a trading post different from a store?
Ellis made a token system to make trades fair. Why did he need that?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: The Full Trading Post (with Token System)
materials: Value cards (index cards, one per item)
Token system: small paper discs or poker chips (10 per student, three denominations: 1, 3, 5)
"Trade Log" worksheet (hand-drawn: columns for Item Given, Item Received, Token Value, Satisfied? Y/N)
Table or desk space for each student's "booth"

steps.title: Booth Setup & Valuation (8 min)
steps.description: Each student sets up their booth. For each item, they assign a token value: small/common = 1 token, medium = 3 tokens, something unique/rare = 5 tokens. Write values on value cards.

steps.title: Token Distribution (2 min)
steps.description: Each student receives 10 tokens (start equal). Tokens represent relative worth, not money.

steps.title: Ellis's Rule Explanation (3 min)
steps.description: Teacher explains: "To make a trade fair, the tokens must balance. A 3-token item trades for another 3-token item, or three 1-token items, or you can negotiate. Both people must agree the token balance is fair."

steps.title: Trading Round 1 (8 min)
steps.description: Open trading. Students must negotiate token values before swapping items.

steps.title: Mid-Point Check (2 min)
steps.description: Pause. Anyone feel they got an unfair trade? How do we decide? Class votes on one disputed trade — was it fair?

steps.title: Trading Round 2 (7 min)
steps.description: Continue trading. Students may re-value their remaining items based on what they learned.

steps.title: Trade Log & Reflection (5 min)
steps.description: Fill in trade log. Total tokens in and out — did you "profit"? Whole-class debrief.

discussionQuestions: Was it harder to trade something you really liked? Why?
Did token values seem 'right' to everyone? What does that tell us about value?
Mr. Mason said 'reusing things means nothing goes to waste.' How is trading better for the environment?
How is Ellis's token system like money? How is it different?
If one item was very popular, did its value go up? What does that remind you of?
extensionIdeas: Run a class-wide trading post for a full week — add new items Monday, trade by Friday
Compare barter to modern "Buy Nothing" groups or Craigslist Free sections
Research: what did people in ancient civilizations trade? What was the first known currency and why was barter replaced?

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: Students bring items from home; classroom supplies for value cards
items: Students bring 1-3 items from home (teacher sends a simple note home at least one day in advance: "bring something you don't use anymore — a pencil, sticker sheet, small toy")

**Backup box:** Teacher keeps a small box of 20-30 tradeable classroom items (spare pencils, erasers, stickers, bookmarks, small notepads) for students who forget or are unable to bring something from home — pull from this box so no student sits out the trading rounds
Scrap paper torn into squares for value cards
Pencils (classroom supply)
Token system: teacher pre-cuts paper circles in three sizes for denominations

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
lowCost.description: Shared supplies that elevate the experience
items: Index cards for value cards (~$0.12/student reusable)
Poker chips or colored counters for token system (~$5/set for class, reusable every year)
"Trade Certificate" printed by teacher — one per student to record their final trade

premium.label: Premium Package
premium.description: Individual materials that enhance the full simulation
items: Small cardboard "booth sign" with student's name (~$0.25/student using scrap cardboard)
Printed trade log worksheet (~$0.10/student)
Laminated "Trading Post Rules" card students keep (~$0.50/student)
Optional: small prize for successful trades (sticker, bookmark, pencil)

focus: Bring one item and make a simple value card (draw it)
Make a fair one-for-one trade with help
Practice: "Do you want to trade?"
Words: trade, fair, mine, yours
Create value cards with a sentence frame
Negotiate a trade both people agree to
Explain why a trade felt fair
Vocabulary: negotiate, value, exchange, agree
Make multi-item trades and justify the value
Compare two offers and choose the better one
Record each trade and whether it was fair
Vocabulary: barter, transaction, worth, compromise
Run a trading post and track all transactions
Weigh value vs. need when negotiating
Reflect on what makes a trade fair to both sides
Vocabulary: supply, demand, transaction, perceived value

title.en: Map It! Classroom Expedition & Blueprint Challenge
title.es: Map It! Classroom Expedition & Blueprint Challenge

description.en: Students create a simple map of their classroom or school, mark "points of interest," and then lead a partner through an expedition using only their map as a guide. The activity builds on observation, planning, and the insight that curiosity — not money — unlocks discovery.
description.es: Students create a simple map of their classroom or school, mark "points of interest," and then lead a partner through an expedition using only their map as a guide. The activity builds on observation, planning, and the insight that curiosity — not money — unlocks discovery.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: One half-sheet of paper per student

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: Ask: "Benny found an old map. What did it help him do?" (Find the creek. Go somewhere new. Discover things.) "Today you'll make a map of our classroom."

steps.title: Draw Your Map (4 min)
steps.description: Students draw a simple top-down map of the classroom from memory — just the major shapes (door, windows, desks, board). No detail required. Label 3 spots with an X: one place that's always useful (e.g., the pencil sharpener), one that's interesting (a bulletin board display), one that most people overlook.

steps.title: Partner Share (3 min)
steps.description: Swap maps with a partner. Can they find all 3 X spots using only the map?

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "What would happen if you went exploring without a map or a plan?"

discussionQuestions: Did your partner's map make sense? What was missing?
Benny's friends didn't know the creek existed. What free things exist near our school that most people haven't noticed?
How is a map like a plan for a project or a purchase?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Full sheet of paper per student
"Discovery Log" (hand-drawn 3-row table: Location | What I Found | Value — free / useful / interesting / beautiful)

steps.title: Make Your Map (7 min)
steps.description: Students draw a map of the classroom AND the hallway outside (or the school common area). Mark 5 Points of Interest with symbols: a star for "most useful," a heart for "most interesting," a question mark for "something I've never looked at closely."

steps.title: Expedition (8 min)
steps.description: Students take their map and walk to at least 3 of their marked spots. At each spot, they write one entry in their Discovery Log: "I found ___. It's ___ (free / useful / interesting). I notice it because ___."

steps.title: Return & Compare (3 min)
steps.description: Back at desks, compare discovery logs with a partner. "Did you notice the same things? Different things? Why?"

steps.title: Whole-Class Debrief (2 min)
steps.description: Teacher asks: "How many of you found something interesting you walk past every day?" (Expect hands.) "That's what Benny did — he found the creek. It was always there."

discussionQuestions: What did you discover that surprised you?
How is being curious a kind of resource? What does it cost?
What free things are in our school that new students might miss?
Benny had a plan (the map). How did having a plan make the expedition go better?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Full sheets of paper (2 per student)
Pencils, rulers, colored pencils or markers
"Expedition Planning Sheet" (hand-drawn: sections for Goal, Route, What I Expect to Find, What I Actually Found)
Sticky notes (for marking discoveries on a class-wide map)
Large class map taped to the wall (teacher draws basic school layout in advance)

steps.title: Plan Your Expedition (8 min)
steps.description: Students complete an Expedition Planning Sheet: "Where will I go? What route will I take? What do I expect to find?" Then draw their map with a marked route.

steps.title: Solo Expedition (10 min)
steps.description: Students explore solo using their map and planning sheet. They're looking for things that: (a) exist but people ignore, (b) are free to use, or (c) they've never noticed before. At each stop, write "Found: ___. Value: ___."

steps.title: Guide Your Partner (8 min)
steps.description: Return. Pair with a partner. Give your partner your map and planning sheet but NOT your discovery log. They follow your map and try to find your top discovery. Can they? What did they find that you missed?

steps.title: Class Map Update (5 min)
steps.description: Each student adds one sticky note to the class map noting their top discovery: "At [location] I found ___ — worth visiting because ___."

steps.title: Planning Reflection (4 min)
steps.description: "Benny's map was drawn years ago. Was it still accurate? Was your map accurate? What makes a plan stay useful or become outdated?"

discussionQuestions: How did having a plan change your expedition compared to just wandering?
Mr. Mason gave Benny a notebook so he could draw his own maps. Why is making your OWN plan important?
The stepping stones across the creek were 'stable' — meaning safe and trustworthy. What makes a plan stable? What makes it unstable?
Benny found the creek because he found a MAP, not because he bought anything. What else do people discover without spending money?
What would happen if you planned a purchase the same way you planned this expedition — making a map before spending?
extensionIdeas: Create a "School Discovery Guide" — a real map for new students showing the best free resources and interesting spots
Design a neighborhood map showing free recreation options (parks, trails, public art, libraries)
Comparison: what did early explorers use as maps? How did they navigate without GPS?

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: Classroom supplies only
items: Paper (classroom supply)
Pencils and crayons (classroom supply)
Teacher draws a base classroom outline on board; students copy and add detail
Discovery log hand-drawn by students on the back of their map sheet

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
items: Rulers for cleaner map lines (~$3/pack shared)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Graph paper for more structured maps (~$0.25/student)
Colored pencil set (individual or per-pair) (~$1/student)
"Junior Explorer" notebook (like the one Mr. Mason gives Benny) for ongoing use (~$1-2/student)

focus: Draw a simple map with a few landmarks
Lead a partner to one spot using your map
Use picture symbols instead of words
Words: map, go, path, here
Map the classroom with labeled points of interest
Guide a partner along a route with directions
Fix the map when a turn is missing
Vocabulary: route, landmark, plan, explore
Map a larger area with a key
Plan and lead a multi-stop expedition
Revise the map after testing it
Vocabulary: blueprint, scale, navigate, legend
Design a blueprint with a key and accurate layout
Lead an expedition and adjust the route on the fly
Explain how planning prevents wrong turns
Vocabulary: orientation, precision, contingency, landscape

chapterTitle.es: El Puesto de Arte de Riley

description.en: Each student identifies one thing they're genuinely good at — not necessarily art, but anything — and creates a "skill card." In a structured Skills Fair, students spend time teaching their skill to a partner. The experience of being sought out for what you know generates the same "full inside" feeling Riley describes in the episode.
description.es: Each student identifies one thing they're genuinely good at — not necessarily art, but anything — and creates a "skill card." In a structured Skills Fair, students spend time teaching their skill to a partner. The experience of being sought out for what you know generates the same "full inside" feeling Riley describes in the episode.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "Riley thought her art wasn't good enough. But Ellis said it was valuable. Today we're all finding our own valuable thing. Think: what is ONE thing you're good at that other people might want to learn?" Give examples: counting fast, tying shoes, drawing animals, knowing dinosaur names, singing a song, folding paper.

steps.title: Create Skill Card (4 min)
steps.description: Students draw and write their skill on an index card: "I am good at ___. I could teach someone to ___ in ___ minutes." Decorate if time allows.

steps.title: Partner Share (3 min)
steps.description: Find a partner. Take turns: "My skill is ___. Here's a quick version of it: ___." (30 seconds each.)

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "Did your skill feel valuable when you shared it? Did it feel different to GIVE it than to show it off?"

discussionQuestions: How is your skill like Riley's art? How is it different?
Does sharing your skill make you have less of it?
What would happen if Riley had SOLD her art instead of giving it away?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Index cards or half-sheets of paper for skill cards (1 per student)

steps.title: Skill Identification (4 min)
steps.description: Students think of ONE skill — specific and real, not vague. "I'm good at art" becomes "I can draw a realistic dog." Teacher models: "My skill is writing really fast. I can teach you a trick for holding your pencil."

steps.title: Skill Card (4 min)
steps.description: Write/draw the skill card: name, skill, one-sentence description, quick drawing showing the skill in action.

steps.title: Teach Session — Round 1 (5 min)
steps.description: Pair with a partner. Person A teaches their skill for 2 minutes. Person B tries it. Switch.

steps.title: Find a New Partner (5 min)
steps.description: Move to a new partner. Repeat teaching round. Notice: is it easier to explain the second time?

steps.title: Reflection (2 min)
steps.description: Back in seats. Write or say: "After I taught my skill, I felt ___. My partner felt ___. My skill has value because ___."

discussionQuestions: Did anything surprise you about teaching your skill?
Did your partner's reaction change how you felt about your skill?
Ellis said Riley's art was worth showing people. Was he right? How did he know?
What happened when Riley's stand was almost empty — did she feel more or less full?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Skill cards (one per student, more elaborate: name, skill title, 3 things they can teach about it)
A half-sheet "Skills Market Passport" per student (hand-drawn: 4 boxes with room for name + skill learned)
Optional: small "thank you" tokens (paper stars) for each student to give after learning a skill

steps.title: Skill Cards — Full Version (8 min)
steps.description: Students complete a detailed skill card: Skill Title, "I can teach you ___," "To do this well, you need to ___," "Here's the hardest part: ___." This prepares them to actually teach, not just demonstrate.

steps.title: Gallery Setup (2 min)
steps.description: Cards are placed on desks. Students do a 1-minute silent gallery walk reading cards — no talking yet.

steps.title: Skills Market Rounds (15 min)
steps.description: Three 5-minute rounds. Each round: students move to one "teacher" they want to learn from. Teacher teaches; learner fills in their Passport. When the round ends, learners rotate. Each student teaches 3 people total.

steps.title: Frances's Flowers Moment (5 min)
steps.description: After the market, teacher distributes "thank you" tokens (or has students write a compliment card for one person who taught them something). Discuss: "Frances brought Riley flowers after the art stand. What is that equivalent to in the Skills Market?"

steps.title: Class Skills Asset List (5 min)
steps.description: Together, create a class list: "Our classroom's skills:" — tally each unique skill. "We have ___ different skills in this room. Together, we're worth ___."

discussionQuestions: Did you value your skill more or less after teaching it? Why?
What happened when multiple people wanted the same teacher? (High demand.)
Riley could have sold her art instead of giving it. Would the lesson have been the same?
What's the difference between a skill you can sell, a skill you choose to give, and a skill nobody wants?
What skill does your family have that saves them money? (Cooking, fixing things, growing food.)
extensionIdeas: Create a "Class Skills Directory" that students add to over the school year — resource for when someone needs help
Explore: what are the most valuable skills in different careers? How do you develop a skill into something people pay for?
Compare: Riley's art stand is free. A commissioned art piece costs money. What changed? When is it okay to charge for something?

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: Classroom supplies only
items: Index cards or half-sheets of paper
Pencils and crayons (classroom supply)
"Thank you" tokens: torn paper strips with "Thank you for teaching me ___" written in class

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
items: Cardstock for skill cards (sturdier, holds up better) (~$0.10/student from shared pack)
Skills Market Passport printed or photocopied (~$0.10/student)
Star stickers for "thank you" tokens (~$2/sheet shared)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Laminated skill card student keeps all year (~$0.50/student)
Printed "Skills Market" passport booklet (~$0.50/student)
Small blank sketchbook or notebook for students to practice their skill at home (~$1-2/student)

focus: Name one thing you are good at
Make a skill card (draw it)
Show your skill to a partner
Words: skill, good, teach, learn
Describe your skill in a sentence
Teach your skill step by step to a partner
Notice a skill you learned from someone
Vocabulary: skill, practice, teach, talent
Break your skill into clear steps to teach it
Give and get feedback at the fair
Explain how skills have value to others
Vocabulary: expertise, feedback, value, demonstrate
Plan a mini-lesson and teach it effectively
Evaluate which skills are most useful and why
Reflect on how skills can be traded or hired
Vocabulary: proficiency, specialization, market value, mentor

description.en: Students run a classroom savings simulation over the course of one week (or compressed into a single session). They "save" virtual or play coins into a class savings jar each day, practice counting and recording, then make a group decision about what to do with the accumulated total — mirroring the friends' debate in the episode.
description.es: Students run a classroom savings simulation over the course of one week (or compressed into a single session). They "save" virtual or play coins into a class savings jar each day, practice counting and recording, then make a group decision about what to do with the accumulated total — mirroring the friends' debate in the episode.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: A bag of mixed play coins (or paper coin cutouts) — enough for 25-30 coins per small group
Paper for recording (one sheet per group)

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "The friends found $4.73 in one week just by looking. Today you're going to count a jar of coins and figure out the total."

steps.title: Sort the Coins (3 min)
steps.description: Each group gets a pile of mixed coins. Sort into piles: pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters.

steps.title: Count Each Pile (3 min)
steps.description: Count each pile. Record how many of each. "We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."

steps.title: Calculate Total (2 min)
steps.description: Add up the total. Teacher checks with the class. Correct if needed.

discussionQuestions: Did the total surprise you? Were there more pennies or more dimes?
If you found 1 coin every day for a year, how much would you have?
What would you do with $4.73 — spend it, split it, save it, or buy something for the group?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Savings Jar" tracker worksheet (hand-drawn: a large jar outline with 7 rows labeled Day 1-7)
Play money or paper coin cutouts
One "class savings jar" (a paper cup or real jar for the teacher to track on the board)

steps.title: Savings Jar Setup (3 min)
steps.description: Each student draws or receives a savings jar tracker. Explain: "Each day this week, you'll save a different amount. Today is Day 1 — save 25 cents." Students draw a quarter in Row 1 and write $0.25.

steps.title: Week Simulation — Compressed (8 min)
steps.description: Run all 7 days in 8 minutes. Teacher calls out each day's "find": Day 1: 25¢ (quarter near the vending machine) Day 2: 10¢ (dime at the park bench) Day 3: 3¢ (three pennies near the fountain) Day 4: 5¢ (nickel outside the corner store) Day 5: 50¢ (found in the wash at home) Day 6: 35¢ (two dimes and a nickel) Day 7: $3.45 (found a whole collection — big find!) Students record each day and draw the coins.

steps.title: Count the Total (4 min)
steps.description: Students add up all 7 days. Compare with a partner. Correct answer: $4.73.

steps.title: The Group Decision (5 min)
steps.description: Read aloud the three options from the story: "Benny said SPLIT IT. Ellis said SAVE IT. Layla said BUY SOMETHING WE ALL SHARE." Class vote. Discuss why people chose differently.

discussionQuestions: Did Day 7's big find change things? What if you'd spent the first $1.28 before Day 7?
Ellis wrote everything in his notebook. Why was that helpful?
Why did Mr. Mason's penny jar story change how the friends thought about their money?
If you save $4.73 per week, how much do you have in a month? ($18.92)

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Play money (coins — pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters)
"Savings Ledger" worksheet (hand-drawn: date, amount found, running total, notes)
Group decision proposal slips (pre-cut paper strips)
A class "savings jar" display (jar on teacher's desk or drawn on board with running total)

steps.title: Individual Savings Ledger Setup (5 min)
steps.description: Students set up a personal ledger: Date | Amount Found | Running Total | How Found. Teacher explains: "Ellis kept records. That's how he knew you're not going to believe this — we have $4.73!"

steps.title: Coin Hunt Simulation (10 min)
steps.description: Teacher has hidden 30 "coins" (paper or play) around the classroom in advance. Students hunt for them. Every coin found gets recorded in the ledger immediately: where found, denomination, running total updated.

steps.title: Count, Sort, and Record (8 min)
steps.description: Class pools all found coins. Pairs sort by denomination and count. One recorder writes the totals on the board. Class verifies the grand total.

steps.title: Financial Meeting (8 min)
steps.description: Teacher facilitates a formal "financial meeting" — three students make proposals (assign roles in advance or take volunteers): "I move that we split the money equally." (Propose how.) "I move that we save it for 4 more weeks and then decide." (Propose what goal.) "I move that we spend it on something the whole class can enjoy." (Name what.) Class discusses pros and cons. Vote by written ballot (secret vote adds engagement).

steps.title: Decision Record & Reflection (4 min)
steps.description: Record the winning decision in the class savings ledger. Ask: "Did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds?"

discussionQuestions: Ellis said 'we need to record this.' Why does writing down what you have matter?
What would have happened if the friends spent their first $1 before they found the rest?
Mr. Mason saved for a whole year. What does that take? What gets in the way?
You voted to ___. Does everyone feel good about the decision? What did you give up?
How is a savings jar different from a savings account? What's the same?
extensionIdeas: Run the class savings simulation for a real week — each day a student "deposits" a token (a real penny or a paper one) and the class tracks the running total
Research: what is a savings account? What is interest? How does a bank use your money while it's saving?
Calculate: if you save $4.73 per week for 52 weeks, what do you have? What could you buy?

Real pennies for the coin hunt (teacher brings a jar; students find and return them)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Individual coin purse for each student to store coins during the simulation (~$0.50-1/student)
Printed savings journal (mini-book format) students keep (~$0.50/student)
A real penny for each student to keep as a reminder of the activity (~$0.01/student)

focus: Add a coin to the jar each day
Count the coins with the class
Draw how full the jar is getting
Words: save, coin, count, more
Record the daily total on a chart
Predict tomorrow's total
Decide as a group what to save for
Vocabulary: savings, daily, total, goal
Track the running total and the days remaining
Calculate how many more days to reach a goal
Explain why saving steadily works
Vocabulary: balance, goal, estimate, progress
Model the savings plan and project the end total
Compare saving fast vs. slow to the same goal
Defend a savings strategy with your data
Vocabulary: projection, interval, target, strategy

description.en: Teams receive identical sets of limited classroom materials and a challenge: build the tallest freestanding structure in a set time. Crucially, teams must draw a blueprint BEFORE building. The planning phase is non-negotiable. After building, they assess: what from the plan worked? What did they find around the room (or in the rules) that helped?
description.es: Teams receive identical sets of limited classroom materials and a challenge: build the tallest freestanding structure in a set time. Crucially, teams must draw a blueprint BEFORE building. The planning phase is non-negotiable. After building, they assess: what from the plan worked? What did they find around the room (or in the rules) that helped?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 1 strip of tape per student/pair (pre-cut, ~6 inches)

steps.title: Blueprint Phase (3 min)
steps.description: Students draw a plan for their tower on one sheet of paper BEFORE touching the other materials. "What shape? How tall? How does it stand up?" Teacher models drawing a quick box-with-layers plan.

steps.title: Build Phase (5 min)
steps.description: Using only the remaining 2 sheets of paper and 1 strip of tape, build the tallest freestanding structure possible. No scissors. Structure must stand on its own for 10 seconds.

steps.title: Measure & Share (2 min)
steps.description: Teacher measures each structure with a ruler or hand-widths. Tallest wins. Show blueprints: "Did your plan match what you built?"

discussionQuestions: Did your blueprint help you build faster or slower?
Mr. Mason said 'before you build, you need a plan.' Were the friends glad he said that?
What would you do differently if you had one more piece of paper?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Materials Budget" card per team (lists exactly what they have): 5 index cards, 4 popsicle sticks, 2 strips of tape, 2 sheets of paper

steps.title: Blueprint Phase (5 min)
steps.description: Teams of 2-3. Draw a blueprint together — must agree before touching materials. Assign roles: one person is the "builder," one is the "holder," one is the "checker" (does it match the plan?).

steps.title: Review Materials Budget (1 min)
steps.description: "Look at what you have. Can you build your plan with exactly these materials? You may NOT get more. This is your budget."

steps.title: Build Phase (10 min)
steps.description: Build the structure using only the materials listed on the budget card.

steps.title: Test Phase (2 min)
steps.description: Structure must: (a) stand on its own, (b) be taller than 6 inches, (c) have a "roof" (something covering the top).

steps.title: Debrief (2 min)
steps.description: Each team shows their blueprint and their structure side by side. "What changed? What did you discover?"

discussionQuestions: Were you ever tempted to grab extra materials? What stopped you?
The friends used an old blanket they found — they didn't plan for that. Did you find any 'surprise' resources?
Mr. Mason said they built the fort 'using only things you found.' How is your structure similar?
What was the most resourceful thing your team did?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Per team (3-4 students): 5 index cards, 6 popsicle sticks or craft sticks, 3 strips of tape (pre-cut, 6" each), 4 sheets of paper, 2 binder clips, 10 cm of string
Blueprint sheet with sections: Top View, Side View, Materials List (what you'll use and how)
"Role Cards" for each team member: Architect, Builder, Quality Inspector, Materials Manager

steps.title: Assign Roles (2 min)
steps.description: Distribute role cards. Each person reads their role: **Architect:** draws the blueprint, makes final decisions on design **Builder:** main hands on materials **Quality Inspector:** checks that the structure matches the blueprint; flags problems **Materials Manager:** tracks what materials are used; ensures nothing is wasted

steps.title: Blueprint Phase (8 min)
steps.description: Architect draws blueprint with team input. Materials Manager lists exactly which materials will be used for which part. Blueprint must be signed by all team members before building begins.

steps.title: Build Phase (12 min)
steps.description: Build according to blueprint. Quality Inspector calls "deviation check" if the build strays from the plan — team must discuss whether to change the plan or change the build.

steps.title: Found Resource Rule (3 min)
steps.description: At the midpoint, teacher introduces: "Mr. Mason's Rule — if you find something in the room that isn't on your materials budget, you may use it IF you can justify why it's a better choice than something you have." Teams look around — what do they see? (Rubber bands? Paper clips? A book as a weight?)

steps.title: Test & Measure (5 min)
steps.description: All structures tested: must stand 15 seconds, must have a roof element, must be taller than 8 inches. Measure. Record on class chart.

steps.title: Debrief (5 min)
steps.description: "Did you use your full materials budget? Did anyone find something they didn't plan for? What was the most resourceful moment?"

discussionQuestions: Your blueprint was the plan. Your materials budget was your financial constraint. How did it feel to work within limits?
If you could have bought anything for $5 to improve your structure, what would you buy? Did you really need it?
Ellis figured out the best angles. Riley arranged branches in patterns. Layla directed. Benny carried. In your team, who did what naturally?
Layla found an old blanket — a found resource that wasn't in the plan. What found resource did you discover mid-build?
Mr. Mason didn't buy anything to help them build the fort. What did he bring? (Knowledge, rope, experience.) What's the value of that?
extensionIdeas: Upgrade challenge: teams must rebuild using ONLY found/recycled materials from home (no purchased supplies)
Design a blueprint for a space in school that needs improvement — present it to the principal or custodial staff
Research: famous struct

title.en: Recipe Math: Cost Per Serving Challenge
title.es: Recipe Math: Cost Per Serving Challenge

chapterTitle.es: La Caja de Recetas de Frances

description.en: Students receive a simple recipe and a price list for the ingredients. They calculate the cost per serving of homemade food, then compare it to the store-bought equivalent. The gap between "homemade cost" and "store cost" is the lesson. Older students design their own simple recipe and calculate its economics.
description.es: Students receive a simple recipe and a price list for the ingredients. They calculate the cost per serving of homemade food, then compare it to the store-bought equivalent. The gap between "homemade cost" and "store cost" is the lesson. Older students design their own simple recipe and calculate its economics.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: "More or Less?" worksheet (one per student — hand-drawn: two columns, 3 comparison scenarios)

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "Frances made bread for $2 that fed 12 people. A store muffin also costs $2 — but it feeds one person. Which is the better deal?" Establish: MORE food for the SAME price = better deal.

steps.title: More or Less? Scenarios (5 min)
steps.description: Teacher reads 3 scenarios; students circle "homemade" or "store-bought" as the better deal: Homemade soup: $3 for 6 bowls = $0.50/bowl. Can soup: $1.50 per bowl. Which is cheaper? Homemade cookies: $2 for 20 cookies. Store cookies: $4 for 20 cookies. Which costs less? Homemade lemonade: 1 lemon ($0.50) + water + sugar ($0.25) = 4 glasses. Store lemonade: $1 per glass. Which costs less per glass?

steps.title: Reveal & Discussion (3 min)
steps.description: Go through answers. Discuss: "Was homemade always cheaper? Why might someone still buy from the store?"

discussionQuestions: Frances's vegetables came from her garden — that made the bread cost less. What if you grew your own food?
Even if homemade is cheaper, what does it cost that we didn't count?" (Time, effort)
Benny said this bread was better than store-bought AND cheaper. Do you think that's always true?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Trail Mix Recipe & Price List" (teacher-prepared handout or written on board):

Recipe: 1 cup cereal ($0.40 from a $3 box), ½ cup raisins ($0.30 from a $2 box), ¼ cup pretzels ($0.15 from a $2 bag), ¼ cup chocolate chips ($0.25 from a $3 bag). Total: **$1.10 per batch. Makes 4 servings. Cost per serving: $0.28.**
"Recipe Math" worksheet (hand-drawn: ingredient | cost | total | cost per serving)

steps.title: Introduce the Recipe (3 min)
steps.description: Display the trail mix recipe. "Today you're Frances — figure out if homemade is worth it. First, estimate: do you think homemade trail mix costs MORE or LESS than $1.50 per serving?"

steps.title: Calculate Ingredient Costs (8 min)
steps.description: Students fill in worksheet: write each ingredient, its cost, add them up for total batch cost.

steps.title: Cost Per Serving (4 min)
steps.description: "Our batch makes 4 servings. How much does each serving cost?" ($1.10 ÷ 4 = $0.275 ≈ $0.28 per serving.)

steps.title: Compare (3 min)
steps.description: Write: Homemade = $0.28/serving. Store-bought = $1.50/serving. "How much do you save per serving?" ($1.22) "If your family makes this once a week, how much do you save in a year?"

steps.title: Tradeoff Discussion (2 min)
steps.description: "What does homemade cost that we didn't add up?" (Time, dishes, shopping for ingredients.)

discussionQuestions: Was your estimate right? Were you surprised by how much cheaper homemade is?
Riley asked Frances 'how much does this cost?' Why is that a smart question?
Is homemade always better? Can you think of when store-bought might actually be a better choice?
Frances's vegetables were free from the garden. What's something your family grows or gets for free that could lower a food cost?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: "Ingredient Price List" (teacher-prepared — 15-20 common grocery items with per-unit or per-serving costs):
"Recipe Design" worksheet: Recipe Name | Ingredients | Cost Each | Total Cost | # of Servings | Cost per Serving | Store Equivalent | Savings

steps.title: Introduce Price List (3 min)
steps.description: Review price list together. "These are real approximate grocery costs. You're going to design a simple recipe — something K-4 could actually make at home — and figure out whether it's a good deal."

steps.title: Design Your Recipe (8 min)
steps.description: Each student designs a simple recipe (3-6 ingredients from the list). Must be something real (a snack, simple breakfast, lunch item). List all ingredients and amounts.

steps.title: Calculate Total Batch Cost (8 min)
steps.description: Fill in cost for each ingredient, add for batch total. Estimate how many servings the recipe makes.

steps.title: Cost Per Serving (4 min)
steps.description: Divide total cost by number of servings. Write it clearly.

steps.title: Compare to Store-Bought (5 min)
steps.description: What would the store equivalent cost? (Teacher provides examples or students estimate.) Calculate the savings per serving. Calculate the annual savings if made weekly.

steps.title: Present Your Meal Deal (7 min)
steps.description: Each student (or pair) presents their recipe in one sentence: "My [recipe] costs $[X] per serving. The store version costs $[Y]. I save $[Z] per serving. In a year, that's $[A]."

discussionQuestions: Did any recipe surprise you — either cheaper or more expensive than you expected?
Frances used vegetables from her garden (free). If you grew one ingredient, how does that change your math?
Benny said the bread was better than store-bought. Is 'better' part of the math? (Satisfaction has value too.)
What's the tradeoff for a recipe that saves $1.22/serving? Is it always worth it?
What's one thing your family makes at home that saves money? Do you know how much it saves?
extensionIdeas: Grocery store field trip or virtual grocery tour: find the cheapest version of 5 items on the price list
Create a "Class Cookbook" of the cheapest recipes designed in this activity
Research: what percentage of American food spending is on restaurants vs. groceries? What's the math behind eating at home?

description.en: Each student receives a "broken" item (a deliberately torn, crumpled, or damaged paper object) and a small set of repair tools (tape, glue stick, scissors, scrap paper). They diagnose the problem, decide on a repair approach, fix it, and then calculate: what would it cost to replace this vs. repair it? The activity builds both hands-on competence and a repair-vs-replace decision-making habit.
description.es: Each student receives a "broken" item (a deliberately torn, crumpled, or damaged paper object) and a small set of repair tools (tape, glue stick, scissors, scrap paper). They diagnose the problem, decide on a repair approach, fix it, and then calculate: what would it cost to replace this vs. repair it? The activity builds both hands-on competence and a repair-vs-replace decision-making habit.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 1 "broken" paper item per student (teacher pre-tears a 4"×6" index card or paper shape — one clean tear)

steps.title: Broken Item Reveal (2 min)
steps.description: Each student receives their torn card. "In the story, Benny's train broke in half. Your item has a problem too. BEFORE you fix it — diagnose it. What's wrong with it?"

steps.title: Fix It (5 min)
steps.description: Using only the tape strip provided, repair the item as well as possible. It should be flat, look as good as possible, and hold together when gently bent.

steps.title: Repair vs. Replace (3 min)
steps.description: Teacher holds up a new index card. "A pack of index cards costs $3 for 100 cards — about 3 cents each. How much did your repair cost?" (Almost nothing — just a piece of tape.) "What did you save?"

discussionQuestions: Was the repair worth it? Why or why not?
Mr. Mason fixed Benny's train instead of buying a new one. Why was that smarter?
What things do you own that could be fixed instead of replaced?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 4 "broken" paper items per student (each with a different type of damage):
Item A: torn (clean tear through the middle)
Item C: a simple paper "frame" with a cut in one corner
Item D: a paper "book cover" with a bent/folded corner and small rip
Repair toolkit per student: 2 tape strips, scissors, glue stick, 1 small piece of blank paper
"Repair vs. Replace" T-chart (hand-drawn on the back of their work area)

steps.title: Diagnosis Round (3 min)
steps.description: Students receive all 4 broken items. Before touching any repair tools: write/draw what's wrong with each item on the back (one word per item: torn, wrinkled, cut, bent).

steps.title: Fix-It Round (12 min)
steps.description: Students work through all 4 repairs using only their toolkit. Challenge: make each item as close to "new" as possible.

steps.title: Repair vs. Replace Chart (4 min)
steps.description: For each item, complete the chart: | Item | What I used to fix it | Cost to fix | Cost to replace | Money saved | Teacher provides replacement costs: index card = $0.03, book = $5-15, frame = $10-20.

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "Which repair saved the most money? Which was hardest? Would you always repair instead of replace?"

discussionQuestions: Mr. Mason fixed Ellis's torn book cover by showing Ellis how to tape it himself. Why did he teach Ellis instead of just doing it?
Was there an item you couldn't fully fix? What would a professional fixer do?
What makes something NOT worth fixing? When IS it better to replace?
Is there something at home right now that's broken but hasn't been fixed yet? What would it take?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: 4 broken paper items per student (as above)
Full repair toolkit: tape (2 strips), scissors, glue stick, scrap paper, binder clip, 1 rubber band
"Repair Report" worksheet (hand-drawn: Item | Damage Type | Repair Method | Cost to Repair | Replacement Cost | Savings | Would I Fix or Replace?)

steps.title: Mr. Mason's Diagnosis Rule (3 min)
steps.description: Before touching any tool, students must write a diagnosis for all 4 items: "What is broken? How did it break? What's the best tool to fix it?" Establish: Mr. Mason always diagnosed before reaching for a tool.

steps.title: Repair Round 1 — Simplest Repair (8 min)
steps.description: Students fix their 2 easiest items. Quality Inspectors review 3-4 students' work mid-round and give one piece of feedback: "The tape is overlapping the edge — that would make it worse."

steps.title: Repair Round 2 — Complex Repairs (8 min)
steps.description: Fix the 2 more difficult items. Students may combine tools (glue + tape + scrap paper patch).

steps.title: Complete Repair Reports (8 min)
steps.description: Fill in full worksheet for all 4 items. Calculate total cost to fix vs. total replacement cost vs. total savings.

steps.title: Repair vs. Replace Debate (4 min)
steps.description: Teacher poses: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it but it will never be as strong. A new one costs $15. You have $15 saved. Fix or replace? Why?" Class debates. No right answer — unpack reasoning.

steps.title: Class Tally (4 min)
steps.description: "Who fixed all 4 items successfully? Who had at least 1 they couldn't fix? What would Mr. Mason say to the items you couldn't fix?"

discussionQuestions: Mr. Mason said 'rushing can ruin the fix.' Did you rush any repairs? What happened?
In your repair report, what was the biggest savings — the item where fixing cost least vs. replacement cost most?
What skills did you use today? What if you could use those skills every time something breaks at home?
Mr. Mason said his grandfather's chair was still standing after decades of repairs. What's the 'chair' equivalent in your home — something old that's been fixed many times?
Is there an environmental argument for fixing vs. throwing away? What happens to things that get thrown away?
extensionIdeas: Start a class "Fix-It Log" — students record one thing they notice each week that could be fixed instead of replaced
Research the "Right to Repair" movement — why do some companies make things hard to fix?
Bring in a real small broken item (with parent permission) and brainstorm the repair approach as a class

items: Pre-torn/damaged paper items (teacher prepares in advance using classroom paper)
Tape (classroom supply — pre-cut into strips to limit use)
Scissors (classroom supply)
Glue sticks (classroom supply)
Scrap paper patches from the recycling bin

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
lowCost.description: Slightly sturdier items for more realistic repair
items: Index cards as the "broken items" (better repair challenge than plain paper) (~$0.12/student)
Printed "Repair Report" worksheet (~$0.10/student)
Binder clips for the repair toolkit (~$0.05/student from shared pack)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Small "fix-it kit" per student: 3 band-aids (for practice patching), 2 binder clips, a small piece of foam tape, a craft stick (~$1/student assembled)
"Junior Fixer" badge students earn after completing all 4 repairs (~$0.25/student printed)
Take-home "Things I Can Fix" card: list of 10 common items that can be repaired rather than replaced (~$0.10/student printed)
