Pick a tool and fix it with help
Show your fixed item
Words: broken, fix, tool, fixed
Diagnose the problem and choose a repair
Fix the item step by step
Tell why fixing is better than throwing away
Vocabulary: repair, diagnose, tool, reuse
Plan a repair approach and explain it
Repair carefully and check your work
Compare the cost of fixing vs. replacing
Vocabulary: maintenance, durable, value, resourceful
Evaluate several repair options and pick the best
Justify fix-vs-replace with cost and value
Reflect on how repair extends an item's value
Vocabulary: cost-benefit, longevity, craftsmanship, sustainability

description.en: Students brainstorm, categorize, and map the free or low-cost resources available to them in their school and neighborhood. Then they build a "borrow vs. buy" analysis: what needs can be met without spending money? The result is a class-built resource guide that has real utility.
description.es: Students brainstorm, categorize, and map the free or low-cost resources available to them in their school and neighborhood. Then they build a "borrow vs. buy" analysis: what needs can be met without spending money? The result is a class-built resource guide that has real utility.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "Riley and Ellis thought they needed to BUY something to stop being bored. Instead they went to the library and found everything for free. Today: what's free at OUR school?"

steps.title: Brainstorm (5 min)
steps.description: Class shouts out things that are free at school. Teacher writes them on the board as a list. Prompt categories if needed: places (library, gym, playground), things (books, crayons, computers), services (teachers, tutoring, nurse).

steps.title: Count & Categorize (2 min)
steps.description: Count the list. "We found ___ free things. Which ones could REPLACE something you'd otherwise have to buy?"

steps.title: Discussion (1 min)
steps.description: "Who pays for these free things? They're not magic — someone paid for them."

discussionQuestions: If you didn't have access to school, what would it cost to get all these things elsewhere?
Ellis asked 'how can everything be free?' Miss Chen said it belongs to the community. What does that mean?
What's one thing at school you've never used that might be useful?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Two large pieces of paper (or whiteboard space): one labeled "Free or Borrow" / one labeled "Must Buy"
Index cards (5 per student — each writes one resource per card)

steps.title: Brainstorm Round (5 min)
steps.description: Students write one free/community resource per index card (at least 3 cards each). Examples: library book, park, school crayons, gym class, playground, fire station (calls are free), friend's bike, community pool. Include things you borrow from neighbors and friends.

steps.title: Sort — Free/Borrow vs. Must Buy (5 min)
steps.description: Students bring their cards to the front. Sort as a class: "Is this free, borrow-able, or must buy?" Cards go on the correct paper. Debate edge cases ("the library is free but you need a card — is it really free?")

steps.title: Our Neighborhood Resource Map (7 min)
steps.description: Together, create a simple neighborhood map on large paper: school at center, then add the free resources around it at their approximate locations (library two blocks away, park across the street, etc.). Mark each with a symbol: 📚 (library), 🌳 (park), 🏃 (recreation center), etc.

steps.title: Reflection (3 min)
steps.description: Count resources on the "Free/Borrow" side. "If you used these instead of buying, how much money could you save in a week? A month?"

discussionQuestions: Was there anything on the 'Must Buy' list that you could BORROW instead?
Miss Chen said you can borrow craft kits from the library. Did that surprise you? What else might the library have that you didn't know about?
Why do parks and libraries exist? Who decided to make them free?
If you had a library card and used it every week, how much could you save in a year?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Large paper for community map (one per class or per team of 4)
"Resource Profile" template (hand-drawn: Name | Location | What it provides | Who can use it | Cost | Hours)
Sticky notes for "I didn't know this existed!" discoveries

steps.title: Brainstorm All Categories (5 min)
steps.description: Teacher writes categories on board. Teams fill in as many as they can in 3 minutes: Learn: library, tutoring, YouTube, teacher's knowledge Play: parks, playgrounds, community pools, school gym after hours Create: art classes, library craft kits, school art supplies Stay healthy: school nurse, community health events Get food: school lunch program, community gardens, food banks Connect: community centers, faith organizations, neighborhood apps (Buy Nothing groups)

steps.title: Resource Profiles (10 min)
steps.description: Each student picks 3 resources from the brainstorm and completes a profile for each (using the template). They must think about: who can use it, what it provides, what it costs (if anything).

steps.title: Build the Class Map (10 min)
steps.description: Teams pool their profiles and add resources to the community map. Each resource gets a location mark, a symbol, and a "saves you ___" note (estimate how much you'd spend on this if it didn't exist for free).

steps.title: "I Didn't Know This Existed!" Sticky Notes (5 min)
steps.description: Students add 1-2 sticky notes to the map marking something they discovered today that they've never used but want to try. These go in a specific corner of the map.

steps.title: The $0 Week Challenge (5 min)
steps.description: As a class, design a hypothetical "Week of Free Activities" using only resources on the map. What would you do Monday through Friday that costs $0? Present one family's week.

discussionQuestions: The library uses tax money. You and your family already paid for it — are you getting your money's worth?
Ellis said 'how can everything be free?' Is it actually free, or is the cost hidden? Who pays and how?
What's the most valuable free resource in our neighborhood that most people don't use?
Could you live an entire month using only free community resources for entertainment and learning? What would you miss?
Mr. Mason says 'the best things in life are free.' Is that true? What's the limit of that idea?
extensionIdeas: Visit the local library and get library cards for anyone who doesn't have one
Assign: "Resource Hunt" — find one free or borrowable resource at home you've never used and report back
Research: what's in the "Library of Things" at your nearest library? (Many lend tools, instruments, games, even seeds!)

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: All classroom supplies; community map on large paper
items: Large paper (butcher paper or taped-together sheets)
Markers (classroom supply)
Index cards or scrap paper for resource profiles
Sticky notes (classroom supply)

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
items: Printed resource profile template (~$0.10/student)
Symbols/stickers for map marking (~$2/pack for class)
Printed neighborhood map base (if your school has one available from the district)

premium.label: Premium Package
items: Printed "Community Resource Guide" mini-booklet students take home (~$0.50/student)
Library card application forms (free from library — teacher requests in advance)
"My Free Week" planning worksheet (~$0.10/student)

focus: Name one free thing in your school or town
Add it to the class map (draw it)
Tell who can use it
Words: free, share, help, map
List and group free or low-cost resources
Mark them on a community map
Decide one need you can meet without money
Vocabulary: resource, free, borrow, community
Categorize resources and map them with a key
Build a borrow-vs-buy comparison
Explain how shared resources help everyone
Vocabulary: low-cost, access, public, compare
Audit community resources and rank them by value
Analyze which needs can be met without spending
Propose how to share resources more widely
Vocabulary: equity, access, allocation, cost-saving

description.en: Students start with equal small "investments" (tokens or paper shapes). Through structured giving rounds, they observe what happens to the group's total when people share freely. The simulation generates the experience Frances describes — giving doesn't deplete you; it generates reciprocal giving and collective abundance.
description.es: Students start with equal small "investments" (tokens or paper shapes). Through structured giving rounds, they observe what happens to the group's total when people share freely. The simulation generates the experience Frances describes — giving doesn't deplete you; it generates reciprocal giving and collective abundance.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 3 tokens per student (paper shapes, stickers, or paper clips — anything physical and countable)

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "The friends grew more vegetables than they could use. They gave them away. In return, neighbors gave them jam, cookies, and flowers. Today we're going to see what happens when everyone shares." Distribute 3 tokens per student.

steps.title: Giving Round 1 (3 min)
steps.description: "Give ONE token to someone you think needs it or would appreciate it. You choose who. You may give to anyone in the room." Observe: every student gives one and (likely) receives one or more.

steps.title: Count (2 min)
steps.description: "Count your tokens. Did you end up with more, less, or the same as you started?" Class show of hands: more / same / fewer. Tally.

steps.title: Discussion (3 min)
steps.description: "What happened? Did giving away one token leave you with less? Why or why not?"

discussionQuestions: Frances said there's always enough when we share. Did today show that?
Did anyone give more than one token? Did they end up with less?
What if nobody gave any tokens — would that be better?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 5 tokens per student (small paper squares, colored paper clips, or poker chips — 3 denominations if possible: 1, 2, 5)
"Investment Journal" half-sheet per student (hand-drawn: 3 rows — Start | After Round 1 | After Round 2 | Final)

steps.title: Setup & Investment Journal (3 min)
steps.description: Distribute 5 tokens. Students write "5" in the START row of their journal.

steps.title: Giving Round 1 — Free Giving (5 min)
steps.description: "Give however many tokens you want to whoever you want. You don't have to give any. You don't have to give equally." After round: count tokens, record in journal row.

steps.title: Giving Round 2 — "Excess Only" Giving (5 min)
steps.description: "Frances grew more than she could use — she gave the excess. This round: give away any tokens you have above 3. Keep 3 for yourself, share the rest." After round: count and record.

steps.title: Count Class Total (3 min)
steps.description: Teacher tallies: how many tokens does the class have total? Did the total go up, down, or stay the same? (It stays the same — conservation of tokens. Point this out. The distribution changed, not the total.)

steps.title: Discussion (4 min)
steps.description: "What changed between Round 1 and Round 2? What does it mean to share only the 'excess'? Frances had 3 full baskets — more than enough. That's why sharing felt easy."

discussionQuestions: Why is it easier to share when you have MORE than enough?
Frances said 'sharing creates abundance.' What does that mean if the total number of tokens didn't change?
What's the difference between giving because you have extra vs. giving when you're barely getting by?
The seeds the friends planted in Frances's garden (Chapter 2) grew into enough to share. What was the 'investment' that made that possible?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: "Investment Journal" worksheet (hand-drawn: Starting Amount | Round 1: Gave | Received | Balance | Round 2: same | Round 3: same | Final | Net Change)
"Investment Card" per student: "My investment in CH02 was: [seeds + time]. My return in CH11 was: [vegetables + community connection]."

steps.title: Investment Card Warm-Up (5 min)
steps.description: Students complete their Investment Card. "Think back to Chapter 2. Riley planted flower seeds. The return was a whole garden. What did she invest? What did she get back?" Then: "Today's simulation shows the same cycle with tokens."

steps.title: Starting Distribution (2 min)
steps.description: Distribute 10 tokens unevenly: some students get 15 (the "abundant harvest" students), some get 8, some get 5, some get 3 (the "scarce" students). Do NOT announce this is unequal — let them discover.

steps.title: Round 1 — Free Market (7 min)
steps.description: Open giving round. "Give however you want to whoever you want. No rules." Record in journal. Observe who gives, who receives, whether inequity narrows or widens.

steps.title: Round 2 — "Excess Rule" (7 min)
steps.description: "This round: everyone identifies their 'need' (a baseline of 5 tokens). Anyone with more than 5 shares the excess first." Record. Does inequity narrow?

steps.title: Round 3 — Reciprocal Giving (7 min)
steps.description: "This round: if someone gives to you, you must give something back — not necessarily to them, but to someone." Record. Observe the chain-reaction effect.

steps.title: Analysis & Discussion (7 min)
steps.description: Compare all three rounds. "Which round felt best? Which reduced the gap between the most and least token-holders? Why?"

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, did the gap between the richest and poorest students get bigger or smaller? What about Round 3?
Frances grew seeds into food. The seeds cost nothing and came from nature. But the investment of TIME changed everything. What does that tell us?
Layla gave away vegetables. Neighbors gave back jam and cookies and flowers. Did Layla end up poorer?
Benny asked 'to who?' when they decided to share. How do you decide who to give to when you have extra?
The class as a whole had the same number of tokens the whole time. So what did 'abundance' actually mean?
extensionIdeas: Connect to real-world abundance: research community gardens, food banks, mutual aid networks — organizations built on the idea that sharing excess creates community resilience
Write Frances's speech from the episode: "You learned about investment and patience" — expand it into a 3-paragraph essay from the perspective of one of the friends
Compare: what would happen in a market economy where tokens could only be traded for equal value, not given? Run Round 4 with that rule and compare the result

standard.label: Standard Classroom
standard.description: All paper-based tokens
items: Paper squares (teacher pre-cuts from colored paper — different colors = different denominations)
Investment journal hand-drawn on blank paper
Pencil (classroom supply)

lowCost.label: Low Cost Additions
lowCost.description: Physical tokens that feel more real
items: Poker chips or colored counters (class set ~$5, reusable) (~$0.20/student)
Printed investment journal worksheet (~$0.10/student)
Small envelopes for storing tokens during counting (~$0.05/student)

premium.label: Premium Package
premium.description: Individual materials that enhance the experience
items: Small "harvest basket" (paper cupcake liner or small paper bowl) for holding tokens (~$0.25/student)
Printed "Seed-to-Harvest" investment tracker students keep (~$0.25/student)
Seed packet memento (fast-germinating flower seed in a small paper envelope to take home and plant) (~$0.50/student)

focus: Start with a few tokens
Give one token in each round
Watch what happens to the group pile
Words: give, share, more, group
Track your tokens through the giving rounds
Notice how the group total changes
Tell how it felt to give and receive
Vocabulary: give, share, abundance, group
Record the group total each round
Explain why sharing grew the total
Compare giving freely vs. holding back
Vocabulary: generosity, abundance, contribute, community
Model the group total across all rounds
Analyze how generosity creates abundance
Argue when giving benefits the whole group
Vocabulary: reciprocity, abundance, collective value, surplus

title.en: My Season 1 Treasure Book & Exhibition Walk
title.es: My Season 1 Treasure Book & Exhibition Walk

description.en: Students create a personal "Season 1 Treasure Book" reflecting on what they've learned across the season. The book has four pages: a treasure they found, a skill they have, a savings goal, and a way they shared or gave. Books are then displayed in a class gallery walk — a miniature Treasure Exhibition. Optional: students receive their own "Junior Explorer" acknowledgment.
description.es: Students create a personal "Season 1 Treasure Book" reflecting on what they've learned across the season. The book has four pages: a treasure they found, a skill they have, a savings goal, and a way they shared or gave. Books are then displayed in a class gallery walk — a miniature Treasure Exhibition. Optional: students receive their own "Junior Explorer" acknowledgment.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 1 sheet of paper per student (folded in half = 4 pages; use 2 pages only)

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "At the Treasure Exhibition, the friends showed everything they discovered, made, fixed, and grew. None of it cost money. Today you're making your own small book showing YOUR treasures from this season."

steps.title: Page 1 — A Treasure I Found (4 min)
steps.description: Students draw or write: "Something I discovered that was free or found (could be from a season activity, could be from their own life)."

steps.title: Page 2 — A Skill I Have (4 min)
steps.description: "Something I'm good at that has value — a skill I could teach someone."

steps.title: Quick Share (2 min)
steps.description: Partners share one page each: "My treasure is ___." "My skill is ___."

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between a treasure you BUY and a treasure you FIND?
What would the Treasure Exhibition look like if everyone only brought things they bought?
What's one non-money treasure you're taking home from this season?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 2 sheets of paper per student (folded and stapled = 8-page mini-book; use 4 content pages)
Cover page template (hand-drawn or pre-printed): "[Name]'s Season 1 Treasure Book"

steps.title: Book Construction (2 min)
steps.description: Students fold and assemble mini-book. Label cover with name.

steps.title: Page 1 — A Treasure I Found (4 min)
steps.description: Draw and describe a free or found treasure. Where did you find it? What makes it valuable?

steps.title: Page 2 — A Skill I Have (4 min)
steps.description: Draw and describe a skill they can teach. What is it? Who could benefit from it?

steps.title: Page 3 — My Savings Goal (4 min)
steps.description: What are they saving toward? How many weeks to reach the goal at $1/week?

steps.title: Page 4 — A Way I Shared (4 min)
steps.description: Describe or draw one time they gave something to someone — time, skill, object, kindness.

steps.title: Gallery Walk (2 min)
steps.description: Books open on desks. Quick walk to read one neighbor's book. One compliment out loud: "I think ___ is a great skill/treasure because ___."

discussionQuestions: Which page was easiest to fill in? Hardest? Why?
The little boy in the story said 'I want to find treasures!' After this season, what would you tell him?
Does your book show that you're 'wealthy' in any way? What kind of wealthy?
What's the most important thing you learned from Season 1 that you'll remember?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: 2 sheets of paper per student (4-page mini-book)
Gallery walk "response cards" (index cards — 1 per student to leave feedback for another student)
Sticky dots or stars (3 per student for "voting" on displayed pages)
"Junior Explorer" certificates (teacher prints in advance — see template below or hand-write)
Optional: any item from a previous activity they'd like to display alongside their book (a repaired paper item, their savings jar tracker, their skill card, etc.)

steps.title: Mini-Book Creation — Extended Version (15 min)
steps.description: Page 1: A treasure I found (with specific story: where, when, why it's valuable) Page 2: A skill I have (with teaching tip: "Here's how you'd learn it in 3 steps") Page 3: My savings goal (with timeline: "I need $___. At $1/week that's ___ weeks. My plan is ___.") Page 4: A way I'm going to share something this week (future commitment, not past)

steps.title: Exhibition Setup (3 min)
steps.description: Books open on desks. Any accompanying items displayed alongside. Students write their name on a piece of paper in front of their "exhibit."

steps.title: Gallery Walk — Exploration (10 min)
steps.description: Students walk the room. For each exhibit they visit, they can: (a) leave a star sticker on their favorite page, (b) write a response card ("What I noticed about your treasures: ___"), or (c) just read and move on.

steps.title: Reading Response Cards (3 min)
steps.description: Students return to their desk and read the response cards they received.

steps.title: Junior Explorer Ceremony (4 min)
steps.description: Teacher reads each student's name and presents (or tapes to desk) a "Junior Explorer" certificate. Name is called, student stands briefly — like Mr. Mason's ceremony in the episode.

steps.title: Class Synthesis (5 min)
steps.description: "In the story, the friends built an entire exhibition without buying anything. Look around this room — what did we make this season?" Make a list together: activities, skills, savings math, repairs, maps, treasure books. "That's abundance."

discussionQuestions: What exhibit surprised you the most during the gallery walk?
The little boy at the exhibition said 'I want to find treasures too!' — who in another class could you share your learning with?
What chapter taught you the most about money? What chapter taught you the most about something else?
Mr. Mason called the friends 'Junior Explorers.' What does that title mean to you after this season?
The best treasures are the ones you discover, create, and share. Do you agree? What's one treasure from this season that fits all three?
extensionIdeas: Present the Treasure Exhibition to another class — students explain one page of their book to a new audience
Create a "Season 2 Preview": "Based on what I learned, here's one financial question I still have..."
Write a le

description.en: The Great Classroom Swap
description.es: The Great Classroom Swap

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Each student brings 1 small item from home (toy, book, trading card, craft supply they no longer want)

steps.title: Swap Meet Introduction
steps.description: Explain swap meet rules: bring one item you're willing to trade, both people must agree, you can say no, trades must be fair. Review what makes trading fair.

steps.title: Trading Round
steps.description: Students circulate with their items and negotiate trades. Encourage respectful communication: 'Would you trade your ___ for my ___?' Track who trades and who doesn't on class chart.

steps.title: Mid-Activity Check-In
steps.description: Pause trading. Quick discussion: What trades happened? What made you decide to trade or not trade? Any surprises? Students can make additional trades if they want.

steps.title: Trading Data Review
steps.description: Look at class trading data: How many students traded? How many trades total? Who didn't trade and why? Chart the results together.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: Discuss: Is your new item better than your old one? What makes a trade feel fair? How is trading different from buying and selling?

discussionQuestions: Did you trade? Why or why not?
Is your new item better than your old one? Why?
What made you want to trade?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Index cards or scrap paper for "value cards"
Optional: small tables or desks for display

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the The Great Classroom Swap activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity
steps.description: Students complete the core The Great Classroom Swap activity. Monitor progress, provide support as needed, and ensure students stay on task. Encourage student engagement and participation.

steps.title: Introduction & Item Share
steps.description: Students sit in circle with their item. Each shows their item: "I brought a ___."

steps.title: Round 1 Swap
steps.description: Turn to partner on right. Decide: do you want to trade? If yes, swap items. If no, keep yours.

steps.title: Rotate & Round 2
steps.description: Rotate three spots clockwise. New partner. Same decision: trade or keep?

steps.title: Round 3 & Final
steps.description: Rotate again. Final trading opportunity.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: "Did you end up with something you like more than what you brought?"

discussionQuestions: Did everyone value the same items? Why or why not?
What made a trade feel fair?
Was there an item lots of people wanted? What happened?
How did you decide what to trade for?
How is a swap meet different from a store?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Swap Meet with Negotiation Practice
materials: Booth signs (optional: made in advance or during activity)

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the The Great Classroom Swap activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity

steps.title: Round 1 Swap

steps.title: Rotate & Round 2

description.en: Lemonade Stand Showdown
description.es: Lemonade Stand Showdown

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

steps.title: Set Up Stands
steps.description: Divide class into 2-3 lemonade stand teams. Each team gets play money, price signs, and 'cups' to sell. Decide on prices: cheap, medium, or expensive.

steps.title: First Sales Round
steps.description: Teams take turns being sellers and customers. Customers have limited play money. Count how many cups each stand sells. Track sales on board.

steps.title: Mid-Activity Discussion
steps.description: Pause to discuss: Which stand sold the most? Why? Was it because of price, location, or something else? Teams can adjust strategy for round 2.

steps.title: Second Sales Round
steps.description: Repeat sales simulation with new customer group. Teams use their new strategy. Continue tracking sales on board.

steps.title: Count Money & Compare
steps.description: Each team counts their total play money earned. Compare results. Discuss: Did the cheapest stand make the most money? Did the expensive stand sell anything? What's the best price?

discussionQuestions: If all stands sell the same thing, how do you choose?
What makes one stand more interesting than another?
Would you pay more for strawberry lemonade than regular?

description.en: Assembly Line vs. Solo Challenge
description.es: Assembly Line vs. Solo Challenge

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

steps.title: Assembly Line Setup
steps.description: Divide class into assembly line roles: cutter, folder, decorator, quality checker. Each person does ONE job only. Set goal: make 20 bookmarks in 10 minutes.

steps.title: Assembly Line Production
steps.description: Start production timer. Paper moves from cutter to folder to decorator to checker. Count bookmarks completed. Emphasis: stay in your role, work steadily.

steps.title: Solo Production Setup
steps.description: Each student gets their own supplies. Set goal: make 5 bookmarks in 8 minutes. Each person does ALL steps themselves.

steps.title: Solo Production Round
steps.description: Students work individually to cut, fold, decorate, and check their own bookmarks. Count how many each person completes.

steps.title: Data Analysis
steps.description: Compare results: How many did assembly line make? How many did each person make solo? Which was faster? Which made better quality? Graph the data together.

discussionQuestions: Which way was faster?
Which way was easier?
Why did teamwork help?

description.en: My Family's Travel Trunk
description.es: My Family's Travel Trunk

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling Total time: 10 min story + 10 min activity = 20 minutes

steps.title: Family Travel Introduction
steps.description: Discuss: Have you or your family traveled? Where? How? Explain activity: create a pretend family travel trunk with items representing places or cultures. Review available materials.

steps.title: Trunk Decoration & Setup
steps.description: Students decorate their box or container to look like a travel trunk. Add labels, drawings of destinations, or maps. Make it personal and creative.

steps.title: Item Selection Planning
steps.description: Students plan what to put in their trunk: drawings of souvenirs, photos from home, items representing family heritage. List or sketch 3-5 items.

steps.title: Trunk Filling
steps.description: Students create or gather items for their trunk: draw postcards, make pretend souvenirs, write travel journal entries. Fill trunk thoughtfully.

steps.title: Trunk Presentation
steps.description: Students share their travel trunks in small groups or gallery walk. Explain: Where would your family go? What's in your trunk and why? What does it tell about your family or heritage?

discussionQuestions: Where does this item come from?
Why is it special to your family?
Did you have to buy it or is it something your family has always had?

steps.title: Introduction (2 min)
steps.description: "Mr. Mason had a trunk with special items from his travels. What special items does your family have?"

steps.title: Think & List (2 min)

steps.title: Draw (5 min)
steps.description: Draw the 3 items on paper. Simple pictures are fine

steps.title: Partner Share (1 min)
steps.description: Turn to neighbor, show drawings, explain one item: "This is ___. It's special because ___."

discussionQuestions: How many different countries/places are represented in our class?
What surprised you about someone else's trunk?
How are our trunks similar? How are they different?
How do items from other places get to us?" (Trade, travel, immigration)

description.en: Spice Detectives: Smell, Sort & Trade
description.es: Spice Detectives: Smell, Sort & Trade

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 5 common spices in containers (cinnamon, pepper, oregano, garlic powder, vanilla)
Numbered containers (paper cups with lids or small jars)

steps.title: Spice Introduction
steps.description: Show variety of spices (or pictures). Discuss: What are spices? Where do they come from? How do people use them? Explain smell-and-guess game rules.

steps.title: Spice Exploration
steps.description: Students smell different spices in containers (cinnamon, pepper, herbs). Try to identify each. Notice: sweet, spicy, strong, mild. Record observations with drawings or words.

steps.title: Spice Sorting Activity
steps.description: Sort spices into categories students choose: by smell (strong/mild), by use (cooking/baking), by color, or by preference (like/don't like). Create sorting chart.

steps.title: Spice Trading Simulation
steps.description: Pretend spices are valuable trade goods. Students 'trade' spice cards with partners. Discuss: Why were spices valuable in history? Why did people trade them across long distances?

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: Discuss: What surprised you about spices? Which was your favorite smell? How do spices add value to food? Where do spices in our kitchen come from?

discussionQuestions: Which spice smelled best to you?
If everyone wants cinnamon but there's only a little, what happens to its price?
Where do spices come from?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 6-8 spices in small containers or bags
Trading cards (each student gets 3 spice packets)

steps.title: Spice Detective Introduction
steps.description: Introduce spices from around the world. Discuss trade routes, how spices traveled, why they were valuable. Explain detective activity: smell, identify, sort, and trade spices.

steps.title: Smell & Identify Challenge
steps.description: Students smell spice samples and try to identify them. Use observation sheets to record: smell description, color, texture, guess what it is. Compare guesses with actual spice names.

steps.title: Spice Sorting & Classification
steps.description: Sort spices multiple ways: by origin (where they come from), by use (cooking vs baking), by intensity (mild to strong), by preference. Create detailed sorting charts or graphs.

steps.title: Historical Trade Simulation
steps.description: Simulate spice trade: students receive spice cards and 'trade' to collect full sets. Discuss why certain spices were worth more. Learn about historical spice routes and economics of scarcity.

steps.title: Spice Market Discussion
steps.description: Reflect on activity: What makes spices valuable? How does smell affect value? Why do people pay more for certain spices? Connect to modern grocery store prices. Discuss cultural importance of spices.

discussionQuestions: Which spices were easiest to trade for? Why?
Which were hardest? Why?
How does rarity affect value?
How did you decide what to trade?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: 10+ spice varieties (mix of common and rare)
Small bags or containers for samples
Market stall setup materials (signs, fabric, etc.)
Optional: Mortar and pestle for grinding demonstration

steps.title: Spice Trade History Introduction
steps.description: Discuss historical spice trade: ancient routes, why spices were valuable as gold, cultural significance across civilizations. Show map of spice routes. Explain extended spice detective investigation.

steps.title: Sensory Exploration Station
steps.description: Students rotate through spice stations: smell, observe color/texture, taste safe samples (if permitted), record detailed observations. Use scientific observation sheets. Compare fresh vs dried versions where possible.

steps.title: Classification & Categorization
steps.description: Students create complex classification systems: organize spices by multiple characteristics (origin, use, intensity, price, cultural significance). Create Venn diagrams or multi-category charts. Research where spices come from.

steps.title: Spice Trade Economics Game
steps.description: Extended trading simulation: students are merchants with different spices. Some spices are rare (high value), some common (low value). Trade to complete orders. Track profit. Discuss supply, demand, and scarcity.

steps.title: Cultural Spice Research
steps.description: In pairs, students research how different cultures use specific spices: Indian curry, Mexican chili, Italian basil, Chinese five-spice. Present findings. Discuss how spices connect to cultural identity.

steps.title: Spice Market Reflection
steps.description: Synthesize learning: Why were spices worth traveling thousands of miles? How do spices connect cultures? What determines spice value today vs historically? Create spice value ranking and justify choices.

What happened when a spice was rare and popular?
Was it easier to buy at fixed prices or negotiate? Why?
How did you decide what price to offer/accept?

description.en: Going, Going, Gone! Classroom Auction
description.es: Going, Going, Gone! Classroom Auction

materials: 5 desirable classroom items (stickers, pencils, bookmarks, small prizes)
Play money ($20 per student - simple denominations)

steps.title: Auction Introduction
steps.description: Explain how auctions work: items for sale, people bid (offer price), highest bid wins. Show bidding paddle. Practice auction calls: 'Going once, going twice, sold!' Set play money budget.

steps.title: Item Preview & Bidding Planning
steps.description: Display classroom auction items (books, supplies, privileges like line leader). Students preview items and decide what they want most. Plan bidding strategy: save money for favorite item or spread out bids?

steps.title: Auction Preparation
steps.description: Students create bidding paddles from scrap paper. Count play money budget. Review auction rules: raise paddle to bid, teacher/auctioneer decides when sold. Practice raising paddles.

steps.title: Classroom Auction
steps.description: Run the auction! Auctioneer presents each item. Students bid by raising paddles. Track winning bids on board. Highest bidder 'pays' play money and receives item.

steps.title: Auction Reflection
steps.description: Discuss: What sold for the most? Why? Did you get what you wanted? What happens when many people want the same thing? How is an auction different from a regular store?

discussionQuestions: What item sold for the most? Why?
Did you spend your money wisely?
What happens when lots of people want the same thing?

steps.title: Introduce Ingredients & Prices (2 min)
steps.description: Show four ingredients. Point to price poster: "Cereal costs 25¢ per scoop. Raisins cost 50¢. Pretzels cost 25¢. Chocolate chips cost 75¢."

steps.title: Mix Trail Mix (3 min)
steps.description: Each student takes 1 scoop of each ingredient, adds to cup, mixes

steps.title: Calculate Cost Together (3 min)
steps.description: Write on board: 25¢ + 50¢ + 25¢ + 75¢. Students help count: "What's 25 plus 50? Now add 25 more." Total: $1.75

steps.title: Discuss Selling Price (2 min)
steps.description: "Our trail mix costs $1.75 to make. Should we sell it for $1.75?" (No, no profit!) "How about $2.00? $2.50? $3.00?"

discussionQuestions: How much did our trail mix cost to make?
Would you buy it for $2.00?
Why do we need to charge MORE than it costs to make?
What could a bakery do with the extra money?" (Pay workers, buy more ingredients, keep lights on)

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: K-1st grade, quick introduction, minimal prep time
20.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: * - 10-15 picture cards showing various items (food and non-food)
Two sorting areas (circles on floor or desk sections)

steps.title: Introduction (3 minutes)
steps.description: Show students a banana: "Fresh today, brown tomorrow—why?". Explain some things last, others don't. Introduce sorting challenge

steps.title: Sorting Activity (10 minutes)
steps.description: Students take turns selecting a card. Place in correct category: Spoils Fast or Lasts Long. Class votes if unsure. Discuss each placement

steps.title: Quick Game (5 minutes)
steps.description: Teacher calls out items. Students point to correct category. Speed increases for challenge

steps.title: Discussion (2 minutes)
steps.description: "Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?". "What happens if you wait to sell milk?". Connect to morning market story Items to Include:. Spoils Fast: fish, milk, bread, lettuce, bananas, strawberries. Lasts Long: toys, books, clothes, pencils, rocks, jewelry

discussionQuestions: Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?
What happens if you wait to sell milk?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: 1st-2nd grade, balanced depth, standard class activity
30.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: Item cards (3 per student: 1 perishable, 2 non-perishable)
Price chart showing rounds and values

steps.title: Setup & Explanation (5 minutes)
steps.description: Each student receives: * 1 perishable card (fish, bread, milk, fruit) * 2 non-perishable cards (toys, books, tools, clothes). Explain three trading rounds. Show price chart on board

steps.title: Round 1: Morning Market (7 minutes)
steps.description: Timer set for 3 minutes. Prices: Perishables $10, Non-perishables $5. Students can sell to "market buyer" (teacher/volunteer). Buyers walk around making offers. Record what each student sells

steps.title: Round 2: Midday Market (7 minutes)
steps.description: Timer set for 2 minutes. Prices: Perishables DROP to $5, Non-perishables stay $5. Students who held perishables see value decrease. More selling happens. Visual: Update price chart dramatically

steps.title: Round 3: Afternoon Market (7 minutes)
steps.description: Timer set for 1 minute. Prices: Perishables DROP to $1, Non-perishables stay $5. Last chance to sell. Those who held perishables feel real impact

steps.title: Count & Compare (4 minutes)
steps.description: Students count final money. Graph results on board. Who made the most? What strategy did they use?. Who sold perishables early? Late?

discussionQuestions: Who sold fish in Round 1? Why?
Who waited? How did that work out?
What would you do differently next time?
Why don't toy prices drop like fish prices?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: Mixed inventory cards (10 items per student: 4 perishable, 6 non-perishable)
Play money ($50 per student as starting cash)

steps.title: Market Setup (8 minutes)
steps.description: Students set up stalls with inventory. Receive starting cash $50. Review price tracking sheet. Assign initial "buyers" (rotating role). Practice using tracking sheet

steps.title: Period 1: Dawn Market (10 minutes)
steps.description: Timer: 5 minutes of active trading. Starting prices: * Perishables: $8 each (fish, fruit, milk, bread) * Non-perishables: $5 each (toys, books, tools, clothes, crafts, jewelry). Buyers visit stalls, negotiate, purchase. Sellers mark sales on tracking sheet. Rotate buyer badges after 3 minutes

steps.title: Period 2: Mid-Morning Market (10 minutes)
steps.description: Timer: 4 minutes of active trading. Price changes announced dramatically: * Perishables: DROP to $4 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Discussion pause: "Notice anything about your fish value?". Continue trading. Sellers see depreciation impact. Rotate buyers again

steps.title: Period 3: Late Morning Market (10 minutes)
steps.description: Timer: 3 minutes of active trading. Final price changes: * Perishables: DROP to $2 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Urgent selling begins. Some students stuck with near-worthless perishables. Close market

steps.title: Analysis & Graphing (7 minutes)
steps.description: Students calculate total revenue. Create bar graphs showing: * Starting inventory value * Final revenue * Difference (profit/loss). Class data: graph average revenue by strategy. Identify patterns: early sellers vs. holders Price Tracking Sheet Format: ``` Name: ________________ Stall #: ____ INVENTORY: Perishables: [ ] Fish [ ] Fruit [ ] Milk [ ] Bread Non-perishables: [ ] Toy [ ] Book [ ] Tool [ ] Clothes [ ] Craft [ ] Jewelry PERIOD 1 (Perish=$8, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 2 (Perish=$4, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 3 (Perish=$2, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ TOTAL REVENUE: $______ Starting inventory value: $______ Profit/Loss: $______ ```

discussionQuestions: What strategy worked best? Why?
Who sold all perishables in Period 1? How did that turn out?
Who held onto fish until Period 3? What happened?
Would you change your strategy if we played again?
Why do real markets work this way?
What items in real life work like our perishables?

description.en: Our Community Garden Blueprint
description.es: Our Community Garden Blueprint

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: K-1st grade, quick introduction, individual design
materials: Paper with grid (or blank paper and ruler)

steps.title: Introduction (3 minutes)
steps.description: Show picture of community garden. Explain: "Many families share one big garden". Everyone helps, everyone gets vegetables

steps.title: Individual Design (10 minutes)
steps.description: Each student gets grid paper (4-6 plots). Draw or place picture cards to "plant" garden. Color different plots for different families. Label with family names or numbers

steps.title: Gallery Walk (5 minutes)
steps.description: Post designs around room. Students walk and observe others' gardens. Notice different ways to organize plots

steps.title: Quick Discussion (2 minutes)
steps.description: "Why is sharing a garden helpful?". "What if you don't have a yard? Could a community garden help?". Connect to La Vecina's garden story

discussionQuestions: Why is sharing a garden helpful?
What if you don't have a yard? Could a community garden help?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: 1st-2nd grade, balanced depth, group collaboration
materials: Large poster paper or chart paper
Grid overlay or ruler for sections
Seed catalog pictures (cut from magazines or printed)

steps.title: Setup & Scenario (5 minutes)
steps.description: Divide class into groups of 4-5 students. Scenario: "Your neighborhood wants a community garden, but gardens cost money". Costs: * Garden plot: $40 * Seeds: $20 * Tools: $20 * Soil: $20. Each student has $20 to contribute

steps.title: Group Investment Decision (8 minutes)
steps.description: Groups discuss: "Should we each make our own tiny garden, or pool our money for one big garden?". Calculate: * Individual: $20 buys very little * Pooled: $80-100 buys full garden with all supplies. Make group decision (guided toward pooling for lesson)

steps.title: Garden Design (12 minutes)
steps.description: Groups draw garden on poster paper. Divide into plots (one per student). Add paths, shared tool area, water source. Select seeds/plants from catalog. Glue pictures in each plot

steps.title: Sharing Plan (3 minutes)
steps.description: Decide: "If tomatoes grow in one plot, does only that person get them?". Discuss fair sharing since everyone contributed. Record sharing agreement

steps.title: Presentation (2 minutes)
steps.description: Each group shows garden design. Shares one thing about their sharing plan

discussionQuestions: Why did pooling money help more than individual spending?
How should you share the vegetables when they grow?
What if someone contributed seeds instead of money—should they still get vegetables?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Large grid paper or poster board (one per group)
Play money ($30 per student in mixed bills)
Resource cards (seeds, tools, soil, water access, time/labor)
Seed catalog or printed plant images
Measuring tools (rulers, tape measures for scale)

steps.title: Scenario Introduction (5 minutes)
steps.description: Present community garden challenge: * Neighborhood has empty lot (12' x 16' = 192 sq ft) * Could become community garden if neighbors invest. Show cost breakdown: * Fence: $50 * Soil (all plots): $40 * Seeds: $30 * Shared tools: $30 * Water hookup: $50 * Total needed: $200. Class has combined $180 in cash (6 students × $30). Gap: $20—someone needs to contribute non-monetary resources

steps.title: Investment Planning (10 minutes)
steps.description: Students receive varied resources: * 4 students: $30 cash each * 1 student: $20 cash + seed packets (worth $10) * 1 student: $10 cash + tools to share (worth $20). Complete contribution worksheet: * Name * Cash contributed: $_____ * Non-cash contributed: _____ * Total value: $_____. Pool all resources in center table. Calculate if goal met ($200 total)

steps.title: Garden Design Phase (15 minutes)
steps.description: Groups (6-8 students) design garden layout: * Use grid paper (each square = 2 sq ft) * Divide into individual plots (4-6 sq ft per person) * Include shared spaces:. Tool shed area. Compost bin. Pathways. Water access point. Assign plots fairly: * Option A: Equal sizes for all * Option B: Larger plots for larger investors * Group decides which is "fair". Select plants for each plot from catalog. Label everything clearly

steps.title: Return on Investment Calculation (8 minutes)
steps.description: Use provided data for expected harvest: * Tomatoes: 20 lbs per plot * Lettuce: 10 heads per plot * Carrots: 15 bunches per plot. Students calculate: * Their investment: $______ * Their expected harvest value (at market price): $______ * ROI: (Harvest value. Investment) ÷ Investment. Example: Invested $30, harvest worth $60 → ROI = 100% (doubled money)

steps.title: Sharing Agreement (5 minutes)
steps.description: Create written agreement: * "We agree that vegetables will be shared by: _____" * Options: equally, by contribution, by need, combination. All group members sign. Post agreements with garden designs

steps.title: Gallery Walk & Reflection (2 minutes)
steps.description: View other groups' designs. Notice different solutions to fair distribution Investment Tracking Sheet Format: ``` COMMUNITY GARDEN INVESTMENT TRACKER Group Name: _____________________ CONTRIBUTIONS: Name Cash Seeds Tools Time TOTAL VALUE ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ TOTAL GROUP INVESTMENT: $______ GOAL: $200 ✅ Met / ❌ Short by $____ PLOT ASSIGNMENTS: Name Plot Size (sq ft) Reason for Size _____________ ________ ______________ _____________ ________ ______________ SHARING AGREEMENT: We agree to share the harvest by: □ Equal shares for everyone □ Proportional to investment □ Based on need □ Other: _______________ Signed: _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ ```

discussionQuestions: Is it fair to give bigger plots to bigger investors, or should everyone get equal space?
What if someone contributed tools instead of money—should they get less vegetables?
How does a community garden help people who can't afford their own garden?
What's the return on investment if you invest $30 and get $60 worth of vegetables?
Could this idea work for other community projects? What else?

description.en: Handmade Holiday Workshop
description.es: Handmade Holiday Workshop

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: K-1st grade, introduction to concept, minimal materials

steps.title: Holiday Workshop Introduction
steps.description: Discuss handmade gifts: why make instead of buy? What makes handmade special? Review available materials for making holiday items.

steps.title: Gift Design & Planning
steps.description: Students choose what to make: card, ornament, bookmark, or simple craft. Plan design and gather materials.

steps.title: Creation Time
steps.description: Students create their handmade holiday items using craft materials. Work carefully with attention to quality and thoughtfulness.

steps.title: Finishing Touches
steps.description: Add details, decorations, or messages. Package if appropriate. Make it special for recipient.

steps.title: Sharing & Reflection
steps.description: Show creations. Discuss: Why are handmade gifts valuable? What does making something for someone show? How is this different from buying a gift?

discussionQuestions: How long did you work on this?
Would a machine make it faster?
Is your handmade ornament special? Why?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: 1st-2nd grade, balanced activity with time tracking
materials: Craft materials (paper, felt scraps, beads, pipe cleaners, glue)
Timer or clock visible to all
Sample store-bought item to compare (e.g., beaded bracelet from dollar store)

steps.title: Setup & Introduction (5 minutes)
steps.description: Show handmade bracelet and store-bought bracelet side-by-side. Discuss differences: "Which is unique? Which looks exactly like others?". Introduce concept: "Today you'll make something AND track how long it takes". Explain time tracking sheet

steps.title: Craft Creation (15 minutes)
steps.description: Students choose a simple craft project: * Beaded bracelet or necklace * Felt bookmark * Decorated card or frame. As they work, they track time on worksheet: * Start time: _____ * End time: _____ * Total minutes: _____. Teacher calls out 5-minute intervals

steps.title: Cost Calculation (5 minutes)
steps.description: Materials cost discussion: * "Our beads cost $3 for 100. You used 20 beads = about 60¢" * "If your time is worth $6/hour and you worked 15 minutes, that's $1.50 of labor". Students add: Materials + Labor = Total Cost. Example: 60¢ + $1.50 = $2.10

steps.title: Comparison Activity (3 minutes)
steps.description: Show store-bought bracelet: "This costs $1 at the store". Handmade bracelet costs $2.10 to make. Discuss: "Why might handmade cost more?" * More time * Unique design * Personal touch * Quality materials. "But does your handmade bracelet have special value to you?"

steps.title: Sharing & Reflection (2 minutes)
steps.description: Partner share: "Show your creation and say what makes it special". Celebrate uniqueness of each handmade item Time Tracking Worksheet Format: ``` NAME: ________________ DATE: __________ MY HANDMADE CREATION: _________________ START TIME: _____ : _____ END TIME: _____ : _____ TOTAL TIME: _____ minutes MATERIALS I USED: □ Paper □ Beads □ String □ Felt □ Other: _____ COST CALCULATION: Materials cost: $ _____ (about 60¢) Labor cost: $ _____ (time × $6/hour) TOTAL COST: $ _____ Store-bought similar item costs: $ _____ My handmade item is special because: _________________________________ ```

discussionQuestions: Which is unique? Which looks exactly like others?
Why might handmade cost more?
But does your handmade bracelet have special value to you?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.bestFor: 2nd-4th grade, comprehensive experience with multiple crafts
materials: Calculators for older students Craft Station Options:

steps.title: Workshop Introduction (5 minutes)
steps.description: Introduce scenario: "You're craft vendors at a holiday market!". Explain stations and tracking system. Show sample finished products. Demonstrate time tracking: start timer when you begin, stop when done

steps.title:
Craft Production
- Round 1 (15 minutes)
steps.description: Students choose one station. Create one item, carefully tracking: * Materials used * Time spent * Quality level (self-assessment). Aim for quality over speed. Teacher circulates, provides support

steps.title: Cost Analysis (8 minutes)
steps.description: Students calculate total cost of their creation: * Materials cost: Use provided price list. Beads: 3¢ each. Felt squares: 25¢ each. Ribbon: 10¢ per foot. Paper/cardstock: 5¢ per sheet. Glue: 5¢ * Labor cost: Time spent × $6/hour (or $0.10/minute). Example: 10 minutes × $0.10 = $1.00 labor cost * Total cost: Materials + Labor. Record on worksheet

steps.title: Pricing Strategy (5 minutes)
steps.description: Introduce pricing concepts: * Cost: What it cost you to make * Price: What you charge customers (must be higher than cost!) * Profit: Price. Cost. Students decide on selling price: * Must cover costs * Add profit margin * Consider quality and uniqueness. Create price tag for their item

steps.title: Comparison & Discussion (8 minutes)
steps.description: Compare handmade items to store-bought equivalents: * Handmade beaded bracelet: $3.50 (took 12 minutes) * Store-bought bracelet: $1.00 (factory made in 30 seconds). Discuss questions: * "Why does the handmade one cost more?" * "Which would you rather receive as a gift? Why?" * "What's the difference in quality?" * "Does the handmade one have special value beyond the price?"

steps.title: Gallery Display & Reflection (4 minutes)
steps.description: Set up mini "market display" of all creations. Students walk through, observe variety and uniqueness. Reflection: "Every item is one-of-a-kind because you made it!" Detailed Tracking Sheet Format: ``` HANDMADE HOLIDAY WORKSHOP. COST & PRICING SHEET Maker's Name: __________________ Date: __________ Item Created: ___________________ Station: ______ TIME TRACKING: Start Time: ____ : ____ End Time: ____ : ____ Total Minutes: ______ MATERIALS USED & COST: Item Quantity Unit Cost Total _________ ____ _____ $_____ _________ ____ _____ $_____ _________ ____ _____ $_____ MATERIALS TOTAL: $_____ LABOR COST: Time worked: _____ minutes Rate: $6/hour = $0.10 per minute Labor cost: _____ minutes × $0.10 = $_____ TOTAL COST (Materials + Labor): $_____ PRICING DECISION: My selling price: $_____ Profit per item: $_____ (Price. Cost) COMPARISON: Similar store-bought item costs: $_____ Difference: $_____ Why my handmade item is worth the price: □ Unique, one-of-a-kind design □ Higher quality materials □ Personal touch & care □ Time and skill invested □ Sentimental value for recipient □ Other: _________________ REFLECTION: The hardest part of making this was: _________________ I'm proud of this because: _________________ If I made 10 of these, it would take _____ hours! ```

discussionQuestions: Why does the handmade one cost more?
Which would you rather receive as a gift? Why?
What's the difference in quality?
Does the handmade one have special value beyond the price?

title.en: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
title.es: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project

description.en: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
description.es: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: K-1st grade, introduction to concept, quick activity
20.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project

steps.title: Introduction (4 minutes)
steps.description: Show two items: a dollar bill and a family photo. Ask: "Which can you buy? Which is priceless?". Explain: "Priceless means so special you could never buy it". Share: "Today we'll draw something priceless to you"

steps.title: Drawing Activity (10 minutes)
steps.description: Students draw something priceless to them: * A person they love (family member, friend, teacher, pet) * A special memory (birthday party, family trip, special day) * Something they treasure (not for its cost, but for meaning). Encourage detail and color. Circulate and ask: "Why is this priceless to you?"

steps.title: Writing Component (4 minutes)
steps.description: Simple sentence frame: * K: Dictate to teacher: "My _____ is priceless because _____" * 1st: Copy and complete: "_____ is priceless to me."

steps.title: Sharing Circle (2 minutes)
steps.description: Volunteers share drawings with class. "This is priceless to me because.". Celebrate diversity of what people treasure

discussionQuestions: Can you buy love at a store?
Is a hug worth money? Why is it important anyway?
What's something you love that doesn't cost anything?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: 1st-2nd grade, balanced depth, cultural connection
30.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
materials: Magazines or printed images for collage
Optional: printed family photo if families consent

steps.title: Value Introduction
steps.description: Discuss value beyond price: sentimental value, memories, who gave it to you. Share examples of items that are special but didn't cost much.

steps.title: Memory Item Selection
steps.description: Students think about special memory or important person. Choose what to create: memory drawing, thank-you card, or story illustration.

steps.title: Art Creation
steps.description: Students create memory art project thoughtfully. Include who/what it's about, why it's special. Add details that show meaning.

steps.title: Story Writing
steps.description: Students write 2-3 sentences about their memory art: who, what, when, why it matters. Practice reading their story.

steps.title: Sharing Circle
steps.description: Students share memory art and stories with class. Discuss: What makes these items valuable even if they didn't cost money? How do memories add value?

discussionQuestions: Why can't you buy the thing you drew?
If someone offered you a million dollars for your [family/pet/memory], would you sell? Why not?
How is priceless different from expensive?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.bestFor: 2nd-4th grade, comprehensive cultural and FL integration
45.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
materials: Quality art paper, card stock, or small canvases
Variety of art supplies (paints, markers, colored pencils, pastels)
Collage materials (magazines, fabric scraps, decorative paper)
Frames or decorative borders (can be hand-made)
Display materials (easels, stands, or wall space)
Cultural resources: images of Day of the Dead altars, book about tradition

steps.title: Cultural & Concept Introduction (7 minutes)
steps.description: Read short book or show images about Day of the Dead tradition. Discuss key concept: "People honor loved ones with priceless offerings—photos, favorite foods, treasured items". Introduce FL concept: Intrinsic Value * "Value that exists inside something, not based on money" * "Things that matter for what they ARE, not what they cost". Examples of priceless things: * People you love (can't buy family) * Memories (can't purchase experiences after they happen) * Cultural traditions (can't buy heritage) * Feelings (love, joy, connection). Students brainstorm: "What's priceless to you?"

steps.title: Art Creation (22 minutes)
steps.description: Students create artwork honoring something priceless: * Theme A: Person who is priceless to me (family, friend, teacher, mentor) * Theme B: Memory that's priceless (special day, tradition, experience) * Theme C: Value that matters more than money (kindness, love, honesty, family). Use mixed media for depth: * Drawing/painting base * Collage elements * Written words incorporated * Symbolic representations. Quality encouraged: this is honoring something precious. Teacher circulates, asks guiding questions: "Why is this priceless? What does it represent?"

steps.title: Museum Card Creation (8 minutes)
steps.description: Students complete detailed museum card: ``` TITLE: _________________________ Artist: ________________________ Medium: ________________________ ARTIST'S STATEMENT: This artwork honors: ____________________ This is priceless to me because: ____________________________________ ____________________________________ REFLECTION ON VALUE: Market value (what you could buy it for): $_____ or ☑ Cannot be bought Intrinsic value (what it's worth to me): ____________________ Emotional value: _______________________ If someone offered me $1,000,000 for this, I would: □ Never sell—it's priceless □ Consider it, but probably say no □ Explain why you can't put a price on it: _______________ ```

steps.title: Gallery Setup (3 minutes)
steps.description: Arrange classroom as art gallery. Display artwork with museum cards. Create respectful viewing environment (quiet, thoughtful). Optional: Add battery-operated candles, flowers for Day of the Dead altar aesthetic

steps.title: Gallery Walk & Reflection (5 minutes)
steps.description: Students walk through gallery silently, reading museum cards. Observe what classmates treasure. Notice diversity of priceless things. Appreciation activity: Place sticky notes with positive messages

discussionQuestions: What's priceless to you?
Why is this priceless? What does it represent?
Can you put a price on nature? Clean air? Friendship?

description.en: Our Community Market Day
description.es: Our Community Market Day

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: K-1st grade, condensed experience, time-limited
materials: Student-made items (one per student from previous activities: paper ornaments from CH10, drawings from CH11, etc.)

steps.title: Market Setup (3 minutes)
steps.description: Arrange students in circle on floor. Each student places their item in front of them. Receive $5 in play money. Explain: "We're having a market! You can buy one thing from a friend."

steps.title: Market Time (10 minutes)
steps.description: Students walk around circle looking at items. Decide what they want to buy. Approach vendor: "I'd like to buy your ___. How much?". Vendor sets price (teacher supports: "What's fair?"). Simple transaction: exchange money for item. Everyone buys exactly one thing

steps.title: Sharing Circle (5 minutes)
steps.description: Return to circle seats. Each student shows what they bought. "I bought ___ from ___ for $___ because ___". Celebrate: everyone traded successfully!

steps.title: Quick Reflection (2 minutes)
steps.description: "What did you learn about markets this year?". "What was your favorite FL lesson?"

discussionQuestions: I'd like to buy your ___. How much?
What's fair?
What did you learn about markets this year?
What was your favorite FL lesson?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: 1st-2nd grade, balanced market experience
materials: Student-made items from season (crafts, drawings, etc.)
Optional: simple baked goods (store-bought cookies to "sell")
"Booth" areas (desks grouped or designated floor sections)

steps.title: Market Setup (8 minutes)
steps.description: Divide class into booth vendors and shoppers (will rotate) - Booth Types: * Handmade Crafts (items from CH10) * Art Gallery (items from CH11) * Baked Goods (cookies/crackers—discuss cost of goods CH07) * Repair Shop (Diego-style—fix broken toys or sharpen pencils for fee). Students at booths: * Arrange items * Create price tags (teacher supports: "Remember labor cost!") * Prepare for customers

steps.title: Market Round 1 (8 minutes)
steps.description: Half class shops, half runs booths. Shoppers browse, decide purchases, negotiate. Vendors sell, make change, track sales. Real-time learning: "My cookies aren't selling—should I lower price?"

steps.title: Rotation (2 minutes)
steps.description: Vendors become shoppers, shoppers become vendors. Quick inventory check: "What sold out? What didn't sell?"

steps.title: Market Round 2 (8 minutes)
steps.description: New vendors, new shoppers. Apply learning from round 1

steps.title: Reflection & Celebration (4 minutes)
steps.description: Count revenue (vendors). Share purchases (shoppers). Quick discussion: "What FL concept did you use today?". Celebrate season learning!

discussionQuestions: My cookies aren't selling—should I lower price?
What sold out? What didn't sell?
What FL concept did you use today?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Variety of student-made items from season activities
Price tags, receipt books, tracking sheets
Optional: simple refreshments for "tamale booth" (crackers/cookies representing tamales)

steps.title: Pre-Market Preparation (8 minutes)
steps.description: Assign roles: * Vendors (60% of class): run booths * Shoppers (30%): browse and buy * Market Managers (10%): help resolve issues, make change, support - Booth Setup by Category: * Handmade Crafts Booth (CH10 items): beaded jewelry, ornaments, cards * Art Gallery (CH11 items): memory art (some for sale, some priceless/display only) * Garden Produce Stand (CH09 concept): shared garden items (real veggies if possible, or representations) * Baked Goods Booth (CH07 cost of goods): cookies/crackers with cost calculated * Repair & Service Station (CH05): fix broken items, sharpen pencils, for fee * Trading Post (CH01): trade items without money. Vendors: * Price items (must justify: materials + labor, or fair trade value) * Arrange booth attractively * Create signs * Assign roles (cashier, sales, inventory)

steps.title: Market Period 1 (12 minutes)
steps.description: Open market! Ring bell. Shoppers browse all booths. Make purchasing decisions. Vendors: * Sell items * Negotiate prices * Track inventory * Provide receipts. Market Managers circulate helping. Real market dynamics occur: * Some items sell out fast (demand!) * Perishables get discount as time passes (CH08) * Vendors adjust prices based on demand * Trades happen at Trading Post

steps.title: Mid-Market Reflection Pause (3 minutes)
steps.description: Ring bell for brief pause. Quick announcements: * "Handmade Crafts Booth is sold out! High demand!" * "Garden Produce dropping prices—perishables!" * "Repair Station has a line—service in high demand!". Market insights create learning moments. Resume shopping

steps.title: Rotation Break (2 minutes)
steps.description: Vendors and shoppers switch roles. Quick inventory: What sold? What didn't? Why?. Price adjustments for round 2

steps.title: Market Period 2 (12 minutes)
steps.description: Reopened market with role rotation. Apply learning from period 1. New vendors may price differently based on observations. Continued trading, buying, selling

steps.title: Market Close & Reflection (8 minutes)
steps.description: Ring bell: "Market closing!". Vendors count revenue, complete tracking sheets. Shoppers review purchases - Whole-Class Discussion: * "What FL concepts did you use today?" * "What surprised you about running a market?" * "How did you decide what to buy/how to price?" * "What would you do differently next time?" - Award Ceremony (celebrating learning, not just profit): * "Best Negotiator" * "Fairest Trader" * "Most Creative Pricing" * "Kindest Vendor" * "Smartest Shopper" * Everyone gets participation certificate!

discussionQuestions: What FL concepts did you use today?
What surprised you about running a market?
How did you decide what to buy/how to price?
What would you do differently next time?

steps.title: Materials Introduction
steps.description: Present 6-8 different materials (wood, cardboard, fabric, plastic, metal, foam, rubber, glass). Students predict which is strongest, most flexible, most expensive.

steps.description: Rotate through stations testing: strength (weight bearing), flexibility (bending), water resistance (drops), texture (touch sorting). Record results on data sheets.

steps.description: Using simple price cards, students discover what each material costs. Create a chart comparing properties vs. cost. Which material gives the best value for different purposes?

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: Write or draw: What material surprised you most? Why do manufacturers choose different materials for different products?
