steps.title: Booth Setup & Organization
steps.description: Students create display booths for their products: arrange items attractively, create signs with product names and prices, make labels explaining what they made and how. Organize workspace to demonstrate making process if applicable.

steps.title: Makers' Faire Presentation
steps.description: Run the faire! Students take turns being booth vendors (presenting their work) and faire visitors (viewing others' work). Vendors explain their products, making process, and what they learned. Visitors ask questions and appreciate creativity.

steps.title: Celebration & Reflection
steps.description: Gather for closing circle. Celebrate accomplishments: what were you most proud of making? What was the biggest challenge you overcame? What did you learn about being a maker? How does making things yourself feel different from buying things?

discussionQuestions: Did you sell your items? How did it feel?
What did you learn about selling?
What was your favorite thing you made this season?

30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Classroom Makers' Faire with Sales Tracking
materials: Student-made items from the season (pottery, inventions, blueprints, decorated boxes, etc.)
Index cards for price tags and "About This Product" cards
Simple sales tracking sheet (tally marks or numbers)
Display materials (fabric scraps, small boxes for height variation)

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the Our Makers' Faire: Season Showcase & Sale activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity
steps.description: Students complete the core Our Makers' Faire: Season Showcase & Sale activity. Monitor progress, provide support as needed, and ensure students stay on task. Encourage student engagement and participation.

steps.title: Shopping Round 1
steps.description: Half the class "shops" with play money while half stays at their booth. Practice: "I'll buy this for [price]."

steps.title: Switch Roles
steps.description: Shoppers become sellers, sellers become shoppers. Continue buying and selling.

steps.title: Count Money
steps.description: Count how much "money" you collected from sales.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: Circle share: "I sold ___ items. I learned how to ___."

discussionQuestions: What sold the fastest? Why do you think?
How did you decide what to buy when you were shopping?
Which product took the most work to make? Did it cost more?
What was the hardest part of running your booth?
What did you learn from this whole season?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Full Makers' Faire with Business Reporting and Season Celebration
materials: Complete collection of student-made items from S3 chapters (pottery, woodworking projects, inventions, blueprints, decorated items, prototypes)
Professional-looking price tags (printed or nicely handwritten)
"Product Story" cards (name, materials, time to make, inspiration, skills learned)
Play money (variety of bills and coins)
Display materials (fabric, risers, booth signs, string lights optional)

steps.title: Introduction & Setup

steps.title: Main Activity

steps.title: Shopping Round 1
steps.description: Half the class "shops" with play money while half stays at their booth. Practice: "I'll buy this for [price]."

steps.title: Switch Roles
steps.description: Shoppers become sellers, sellers become shoppers. Continue buying and selling.

steps.title: Count Money
steps.description: Count how much "money" you collected from sales.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: Circle share: "I sold ___ items. I learned how to ___."

discussionQuestions: What strategies did you use to attract customers to your booth?
Which products sold out? What made them popular?
How did your pricing compare to others? Was yours higher or lower? Why?
Looking at your profit, was your business successful?
If you did this faire again, what would you do differently?
Which skill you learned this season (woodworking, pottery, invention, design) was most valuable?
How did the market research from CH10 help you know what to make?
What's the difference between revenue and profit? Why does that matter?

title.en: Solo Challenge: Can You Do It All Alone?
title.es: Solo Challenge: Can You Do It All Alone?

description.en: Solo Challenge: Can You Do It All Alone?
description.es: Solo Challenge: Can You Do It All Alone?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 3 task stations per student: drawing paper, folding paper (origami or paper airplanes), organizing supplies (blocks or crayons)

steps.title: Solo Challenge Introduction
steps.description: Introduce 3 tasks students must complete alone: 1) Write name in bubble letters, 2) Stack 10 books tallest to shortest, 3) Create paper airplane. No help allowed.

steps.title: Task 1: Name Art
steps.description: Students work individually on bubble letters. Monitor but don't help. Students problem-solve independently.

steps.title: Task 2 & 3: Organizing & Creating
steps.description: Students complete book stacking and airplane tasks. Continue working independently. Raise hand when all 3 tasks done.

steps.title: Discussion & Data
steps.description: Count how many finished. Discuss: What was hardest? What did you wish you had? Would it be easier with a partner? Chart responses.

discussionQuestions: Did anyone finish everything? How did you feel?
If you could only pick ONE task, which would it be? What happens to the others?
How is this like the story when Riley kept remaking mugs while Ellis was walking across town?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Solo vs. Team Challenge with Productivity Tracking
materials: 4 task stations: poster drawing, paper airplane folding, supply organizing, price list writing

steps.title: Solo Challenge Setup
steps.description: Explain extended solo challenge: 5 tasks to complete independently. Review all tasks and success criteria. Set time limit: 18 minutes.

steps.title: Independent Work Phase 1
steps.description: Students work on first 3 tasks without help: writing, organizing, creating. Monitor progress but don't assist. Encourage problem-solving.

steps.title: Independent Work Phase 2
steps.description: Students complete remaining 2 tasks independently. Continue self-directed work. Some may finish early, others may not complete all tasks.

steps.title: Results Analysis
steps.description: Count completions. Chart: which tasks were hardest? Create class data graph. Discuss what made solo work challenging.

steps.title: Solo vs Team Discussion
steps.description: Reflect: When is working alone good? When do we need help? What are benefits and challenges of solo work vs. teamwork?

discussionQuestions: Which was less stressful - doing everything or specializing in one thing?
How much more did we produce as a team?
Why do you think Ellis said 'I walk more than I work'?
When might working alone be better than working with others?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Solo-to-Partnership Simulation with Financial Analysis
materials: 5 task stations (drawing, folding, organizing, writing, decorating)
Detailed tracking sheets with time logs
Large chart paper for class data visualization

steps.title: Complex Solo Challenge Introduction
steps.description: Introduce ambitious solo challenge: 7 tasks requiring different skills. Explain: this simulates running a business alone. Set 25-minute time limit.

steps.title: Planning Phase
steps.description: Students review all 7 tasks and plan approach: which to do first, which will take longest, which might be hardest. Create task order strategy.

steps.title: Solo Work Phase 1
steps.description: Students begin working through task list independently. Complete easier/quicker tasks first or hardest tasks first, depending on strategy chosen.

steps.title: Solo Work Phase 2
steps.description: Continue independent work on remaining tasks. Push through challenges without help. Some students will complete all tasks, others won't.

steps.title: Comprehensive Results Analysis
steps.description: Analyze data: completion rates per task, total tasks completed, time management effectiveness. Create detailed charts and graphs.

steps.title: Solo Work Deep Reflection
steps.description: Discuss: What did this experience teach about working alone? When is independence important in business? What did you learn about yourself? How does this relate to entrepreneurship?

discussionQuestions: Who made more money working solo or in partnership? Why?
How did your stress level change between rounds?
What are the ADVANTAGES of working alone? What are the DISADVANTAGES?
In the story, the friends made less than $2/hour working alone. How could working together help?
Why do real businesses have many employees instead of one person doing everything?
What jobs REQUIRE teams? What jobs can be done alone?
extensionIdeas: Calculate class total: sum all solo earnings vs. all partnership earnings
visualize the difference
Research real businesses: how do they divide labor? (Restaurant: chef, server, cashier, dishwasher)
Write reflection: "When I tried to do everything alone, I felt... When I worked with a team, I felt..."
Connect to Season 3: "At the Makers' Faire, did the friends work alone or together? How did that help?"

description.en: Write Your Mini Business Plan
description.es: Write Your Mini Business Plan

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Simple one-page business plan template (photocopied or drawn on board)
Optional: example business names on cards for inspiration

steps.title: Business Plan Introduction
steps.description: Explain business plan: document describing what business will do and how. Review simple business plan template: What will you sell? Who will buy? How much will it cost? Discuss examples.

steps.title: Business Idea Development
steps.description: Students brainstorm simple business ideas: selling bookmarks, offering classroom helper service, making greeting cards. Choose one idea. Answer key questions: What exactly is your product or service? Why would people want it?

steps.title: Customer & Pricing Planning
steps.description: Students identify their customers: Who would buy this? Why? Decide on price: How much would you charge? Why that amount? Is it fair? Would customers pay it? Write down customer description and price.

steps.title: Business Plan Writing
steps.description: Students complete simple business plan template: Business name, what you sell, who will buy it, price, materials needed. Draw picture of product or service. Write 2-3 sentences explaining the business.

steps.title: Business Plan Presentation
steps.description: Students share business plans in pairs or small groups. Explain: What's your business? Why would it work? Get quick feedback: Would you be a customer? Any suggestions?

discussionQuestions: Why did Mr. Mason want the friends to make a plan?
What's the difference between cost and price?
Why does everyone need a job in the business?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: One-Page Business Plan with Pricing Calculations
materials: Business plan template with sections: Name, Products, Costs, Prices, Profit, Roles, Customers
Simple calculator or hundreds chart for math support
Sample cost lists (optional: pretend prices for clay, wood, paper, etc.)

steps.title: Business Planning Introduction
steps.description: Review business plan components: product/service, customers, pricing, materials, costs. Show detailed template. Discuss what makes a strong business plan.

steps.title: Market Research & Idea Development
steps.description: Students brainstorm multiple business ideas. For each, consider: Who would buy? Why? How much would it cost to make? What's the competition? Choose best idea.

steps.title: Detailed Planning
steps.description: Students complete comprehensive business plan: product description, target customers, pricing strategy with justification, materials list with costs, expected profit, competition analysis.

steps.title: Financial Projections
steps.description: Students calculate: cost to make product, selling price, profit per item, how many sales needed to break even. Create simple financial forecast.

steps.title: Peer Review & Refinement
steps.description: Exchange business plans with partner. Give feedback: Is it clear? Realistic? Missing anything? Revise plans based on feedback.

discussionQuestions: How did you decide what to charge for your product?
What happens if your price is LOWER than your cost?
Why did Layla make a RESERVE jar? What's that for?
How did you decide who does which job?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Business Plan with Multi-Product Pricing and Investor Pitch
materials: Comprehensive business plan template with all sections from story
Sample materials cost sheet (wood: $4, clay: $3, paint: $2, etc.)
Chart paper or poster board for final presentation

steps.title: Comprehensive Business Planning Introduction
steps.description: Explore professional business plans: structure, detail level, financial projections. Discuss what investors look for. Introduce comprehensive planning project.

steps.title: Market Analysis & Research
steps.description: Students conduct market research: Who are potential customers? What do they need? What exists already? Survey classmates. Analyze data to find market opportunity.

steps.title: Product Development & Differentiation
steps.description: Develop detailed product/service concept: What makes it unique? Why better than competition? What's the value proposition? Create product sketch or prototype plan.

steps.title: Financial Planning Deep Dive
steps.description: Comprehensive financial plan: itemized cost breakdown, pricing strategy, profit margin calculations, break-even analysis, sales forecasts. Create detailed budget.

steps.title: Business Plan Finalization
steps.description: Complete full written business plan with all sections: executive summary, product description, market analysis, financial projections, timeline. Professional formatting.

steps.title: Plan Presentations & Feedback
steps.description: Present business plans to class or small groups. Practice pitch: clear, persuasive, data-driven. Receive feedback for improvements.

discussionQuestions: What was the hardest part of making your business plan?
How did calculating costs change your pricing decisions?
In the story, Mr. Mason taught PRICE - COST = PROFIT. Why is this formula so important?
Why do you think Layla wanted order forms and pricing sheets written down?
What could go wrong if you DON'T make a plan first?" (Connect to Benny's mistake in CH1)
How does having clear roles prevent confusion and arguments?
extensionIdeas: Compare your business plan to a real kid business (lemonade stand, craft sale, dog walking)
Research: What business plans do adult businesses need? (Permits, insurance, marketing plans)
Create order form template like Layla made
Calculate: How many products would you need to sell to make $100 profit?

title.en: Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store
title.es: Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store

description.en: Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store
description.es: Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 5-10 simple items (classroom supplies, book fair books, or pretend items)

steps.title: Grand Opening Preparation
steps.description: Review classroom store concept: sell simple items (pencils, bookmarks, erasers) using play money. Discuss store roles: cashier, stocker, customer. Set up store area with items and price tags.

steps.title: Store Operations
steps.description: Run the classroom store! Students rotate through roles: being cashier (taking money, making change), stocking shelves, and being customers (shopping, paying). Practice transactions with play money. Track sales.

steps.title: Sales Analysis
steps.description: Students count sales: How many items sold? What was most popular? How much play money collected? Create simple sales chart showing which items sold best. Discuss what made items popular.

steps.title: Reflection & Improvements
steps.description: Discuss store operations: What went smoothly? What was confusing? What would make the store better? If you ran this store again, what would you change? How is running a store different from being a customer?

discussionQuestions: How did it feel to be the shopkeeper?
Did you count the money correctly?
What would happen if we didn't write anything down?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 15-20 items with price tags (mix of low $2-5 and high $10-15 prices)

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity
steps.description: Students complete the core Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store activity. Monitor progress, provide support as needed, and ensure students stay on task. Encourage student engagement and participation.

steps.title: Practice Buying
steps.description: Students take turns buying one item. Practice: "I'd like to buy this." Count out money. Shopkeeper counts and says "Thank you."

steps.title: Role Reversal
steps.description: Student volunteers become shopkeepers. Others shop. Focus on polite transactions.

steps.title: Quick Count
steps.description: Count total money in "register." How much did the store make?

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: "What did you buy? Was it easy or hard to count money?"

discussionQuestions: Which items were easiest to sell? Why do you think that is?
Did the total money match your transaction log?
What was hardest about being the shopkeeper?
How did you decide what to buy?
What happened when you ran out of money?

45.activityName: Complete Store Operation with Profit Analysis
materials: 25-30 items organized by "department" (books, supplies, crafts, toys)

steps.description: Teacher reads aloud: "A customer says your drawing has the wrong colors. What do you say?"

steps.title: Partner Discussion
steps.description: Turn to partner. Decide together: What's the BEST thing to say? What's the WORST thing to say?

steps.title: Second Scenario
steps.description: Quick repeat with new scenario. Faster decision-making.

discussionQuestions: Why did Riley's beautiful plate get rejected even though it was good quality?
What questions should Riley have asked BEFORE painting the plate?

What does 'the customer is always right' mean? Are they REALLY always right?
How can one unhappy customer hurt your business even if you fix their problem?
What's the difference between a refund, a redo, and a discount?
If you handle a complaint really well, can that customer become MORE loyal than before?
extensionIdeas: Write "apology letters" for different complaint scenarios

Track: How many complaints does your favorite store/restaurant handle? Interview staff.

description.en: Competing Businesses: Differentiation Game
description.es: Competing Businesses: Differentiation Game

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 2 "stores" (desks or tables with signs: Store A and Store B)
Simple products to "sell" (paper bookmarks, stickers, or drawings)
Chart paper or whiteboard for tracking

steps.title: Store Setup
steps.description: Divide class in half. Each side is a store selling the same items (pencils, erasers, bookmarks). Both stores set same prices. Emphasize: prices are identical.

steps.title: Differentiation Challenge
steps.description: Give stores 3 minutes to make their store different WITHOUT changing prices. Options: better signs, friendly greeting, organized display, sample item, etc.

steps.title: Shopping Round
steps.description: Teacher and volunteers act as customers with play money. Customers choose which store to visit. Stores track how many customers they get. No price changes allowed.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.description: Count customers for each store. Discuss: Which store got more customers? Why? What made you choose one store over the other? List factors on board.

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, why did both stores end up making almost no money?
In Round 2, did price matter as much? What else mattered?
Would you rather buy the cheapest thing or something special that costs a little more?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Product samples (can be imaginary: paper menus, drawn items)

steps.title: Store Setup
steps.description: Divide class in half. Each side is a store selling the same items (pencils, erasers, bookmarks). Both stores set same prices. Emphasize: prices are identical.

steps.title: Differentiation Challenge
steps.description: Give stores 3 minutes to make their store different WITHOUT changing prices. Options: better signs, friendly greeting, organized display, sample item, etc.

steps.title: Shopping Round
steps.description: Teacher and volunteers act as customers with play money. Customers choose which store to visit. Stores track how many customers they get. No price changes allowed.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.description: Count customers for each store. Discuss: Which store got more customers? Why? What made you choose one store over the other? List factors on board.

discussionQuestions: What happened to profit in Round 1 when everyone kept lowering prices?
What differentiations did teams add in Round 2?
Would you pay more for something if it came with a guarantee or was made just for you?
How is this like the story where Neville's cheap shelf fell, but Ellis's quality work lasted?
What does 'competitive advantage' mean?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Product materials (craft supplies, printed "goods," or menus)
Chart paper for data tracking and graphing

steps.title: Market Setup
steps.description: Divide class into 6-8 competing businesses selling similar products. Each team gets identical starting inventory and play money. Explain: you must attract customers away from competitors.

steps.title: Round 1: Price Competition
steps.description: Teams can only compete on price. Customers (rotating students) shop for best deals. Track sales. Debrief: What happened to prices? (Race to the bottom.) Did anyone make profit?

steps.title: Round 2: Differentiation
steps.description: Now teams can change their product — add features, improve packaging, offer bundles, create loyalty cards. Same shopping period. Track sales and compare to Round 1.

steps.title: Round 3: Full Competition
steps.description: Teams can use price, differentiation, AND customer service. Introduce advertising (30-second pitches). Final shopping round. Track all transactions.

steps.title: Market Analysis
steps.description: Calculate profit/loss for each round. Chart class results. Discuss: Which strategy worked best? Why do some businesses succeed while others fail? What made customers switch?

steps.title: Reflection & Real-World Connections
steps.description: Name two real businesses that compete with each other. How do they differentiate? Write one lesson learned about competition that you could use if you started a business.

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, what happened to businesses that just kept lowering prices?
Give an example of a differentiation strategy a team used.
Did customers care about differentiation, or did they only want the cheapest option?
How is profit margin different from total revenue?
Connect to the story: Why did Ellis decide to RAISE prices instead of lowering them?
What was Maplewood Makers' competitive advantage? (Quality, guarantees, customer relationships)
Real world: Can you think of businesses that charge MORE but people still buy from them? (Apple, Starbucks, etc.) Why?
What's the risk of always being the cheapest option in your market?
extensionIdeas: Research real-world examples of differentiation (Southwest Airlines: friendly service; Volvo: safety; In-N-Out Burger: fresh ingredients)
Create advertising campaigns highlighting each team's competitive advantage
Write business case studies: "When [Team Name] competed on price, profit was $X. When they differentiated with [strategy], profit became $Y."
Graph long-term scenarios: "If you make $1 profit per item vs. $4 profit per item, how many must you sell to earn $100?"
Debate: "Should businesses ever compete primarily on price? When might that strategy make sense?"

title.en: True Cost Detective: Finding Hidden Expenses
title.es: True Cost Detective: Finding Hidden Expenses

description.en: True Cost Detective: Finding Hidden Expenses
description.es: True Cost Detective: Finding Hidden Expenses

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Picture cards or real items (cookies, lemonade cup, handmade bracelet)

steps.title: Scenario Introduction
steps.description: Present scenario: 'You're selling lemonade for $1 per cup. You made $10. Did you make $10 profit?' Students predict yes or no. Explain: profit is what's LEFT after costs.

steps.title: Brainstorm Hunt
steps.description: Students brainstorm all hidden costs for lemonade stand: lemons, sugar, cups, ice, table, sign, time. List on board. Estimate cost for each item.

steps.title: Calculate True Profit
steps.description: Add up all costs. Subtract from $10 revenue. Calculate true profit. Chart: Revenue ($10) - Costs ($___) = Profit ($___). Discuss surprise results.

steps.title: Quick Reflection
steps.description: Ask: Why do people forget about hidden costs? What's the most surprising cost? How could you reduce costs?

discussionQuestions: What hidden costs did we find?
Why do things cost more than just the materials?
Which hidden cost surprised you most?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 3-4 simple products (real or pictures): cookie, paper airplane, friendship bracelet, lemonade

Cost cards (pre-made or written on board)

steps.title: Scenario Introduction
steps.description: Present scenario: 'You're selling lemonade for $1 per cup. You made $10. Did you make $10 profit?' Students predict yes or no. Explain: profit is what's LEFT after costs.

steps.title: Quick Reflection

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between material cost and true cost?
Which category had the most hidden costs?
Why do businesses need to count ALL costs, not just materials?
What happens if you only count material costs when setting your price?

45.label: 45 Minutes

materials: Bulk buying comparison cards (small pack vs. large pack with prices)
PROFIT jar and COSTS jar (labeled containers)

steps.title: Business Scenario Setup
steps.description: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit.

steps.title: Cost Category Brainstorm
steps.description: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.

steps.title: Cost Estimation Activity
steps.description: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using provided price sheet. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record in cost tracking worksheet.

steps.title: Bulk Buying Investigation
steps.description: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. bag of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra)

steps.title: Creating Overhead Tracking System
steps.description: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.

steps.title: Profit Calculation & Reflection
steps.description: Calculate final profit: Revenue - Direct Costs - Overhead - Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between overhead and material costs?
Why do we need a RESERVE jar for future tool replacement?
How does bulk buying change your true cost over time?
What happens to businesses that don't count hidden costs?
Is it 'bad' to discover hidden costs? Or is it helpful to know the truth?
How much overhead should we add to our prices? 10%? 20%? How do we decide?
extensionIdeas: Track a week of classroom hidden costs (markers that dry out, paper waste, electricity for lights)
Research real business overhead percentages by industry (restaurants 30-40%, retail 20-30%)
Create a "Reserve Fund Calculator" for different business scenarios
Visit a local business and interview owner about their overhead costs
Calculate true cost of a school fundraiser (bake sale, car wash, etc.)

description.en: Order Overload: Priority & Delegation Simulation
description.es: Order Overload: Priority & Delegation Simulation

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 5 task cards per student (simple tasks: draw a star, write your name 3 times, count to 20, fold a paper airplane, stack 10 blocks)

steps.title: Order Overload Introduction
steps.description: Discuss business challenge: when you get too many orders at once. Explain simulation: students will receive multiple task cards at once and must decide what to do first. Review concepts: priority, delegation, time management.

steps.title: Task Assignment & Planning
steps.description: Students receive stack of task cards (simple classroom tasks: organize bookshelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers, etc.). Read all tasks. Decide: Which is most urgent? Which takes longest? Which should go first? Make priority list.

steps.title: Task Completion Rush
steps.description: Students work through their tasks in priority order. Set timer. Try to complete as many as possible. If working in pairs, practice delegating: 'You do this one, I'll do that one.' Track what gets done.

steps.title: Reflection & Strategy Discussion
steps.description: Review results: What got done? What didn't? What happened when too many tasks came at once? Discuss strategies: prioritizing urgent tasks, delegating to helpers, saying no to new orders. How do businesses handle rush times?

discussionQuestions: How did it feel to have too many tasks?
Did you finish everything? Why or why not?
Would teamwork have helped?
Like Benny, what happens when we say yes to too much?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 10 task cards per team (mix of quick/long, important/less important tasks)
Task tracking sheets (checkboxes for each task)

steps.title: Solo Overload Round
steps.description: Each student gets 8-10 task cards (draw, fold, sort, count, write, build). Timer starts — complete as many as possible alone in 4 minutes. Count completed tasks.

steps.title: Priority Matrix Lesson
steps.description: Introduce urgent vs. important matrix. Students sort their incomplete tasks: Which HAD to be done first? Which could wait? Which could be skipped entirely?

steps.title: Delegation Round
steps.description: Same tasks, but now in teams of 3-4. Assign roles based on skills. Timer starts — how many more tasks get completed? Compare solo vs. team results.

steps.title: Financial Analysis
steps.description: Assign dollar values to each task. Calculate: revenue from completed tasks minus cost of team wages. Was it more profitable to work alone (free labor, fewer tasks) or hire help (costs money, more output)?

steps.title: Business Scaling Discussion
steps.description: Real-world connection: Why do businesses hire employees? When does it make sense to stay small? Groups create a simple hiring plan showing when to add each team member and what they'd do.

steps.title: Reflection & Journaling
steps.description: Write: What surprised you about working alone vs. in a team? When is it smart to ask for help in real life? What skill would you want to hire someone for if you ran a business?

steps.title: Cleanup
steps.description: Return task cards and materials. Share one takeaway with a partner.

discussionQuestions: Which round felt more stressful?
What strategies helped in Round 2?
How is this like what happened to Benny and his team?
What's the difference between being busy and being productive?
When should we say no to new work?

45.activityName: Full Business Overload Simulation with Financial Analysis
materials: 15 task cards per team with time estimates and payment values

How did the priority matrix help you decide what to do?
What happened to quality when you rushed?
If you were Benny, how would you tell Mrs. Garcia 'not right now'?

description.en: Pivot Challenge: Adapt Your Business
description.es: Pivot Challenge: Adapt Your Business

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 1 scenario card per student (printed or teacher reads aloud)

steps.title: Pivot Challenge Introduction
steps.description: Explain 'pivot': when a business changes its product or approach because original plan isn't working. Discuss real examples: lemonade stand switches to hot chocolate when it's cold. Introduce challenge scenario.

steps.title: Original Business Setup
steps.description: Students start simple classroom business: selling bookmarks, offering helper services, or making cards. Set up, create product, prepare to sell. Begin initial sales or service.

steps.title: Challenge Announcement
steps.description: Teacher announces a problem: 'No one wants bookmarks today!' or 'We ran out of key materials!' Students must pivot: What could you sell instead with materials you have? What different service could you offer? Quick brainstorm.

steps.title: Pivot Implementation
steps.description: Students quickly change their business: create new product, switch to different service, or modify original offering. Adapt with available resources. Resume sales or service with new approach.

steps.title: Pivot Reflection
steps.description: Discuss: Was it hard to pivot? What helped you think of new ideas? Did the pivot work? When should businesses pivot vs. stick with original plan? How do businesses know when to change?

discussionQuestions: What did you change about the business?
Would that help? Why?
Is it better to quit or to try something new?

steps.title: Share Solutions

discussionQuestions: What was wrong with the business before?
What did you change to fix it?
How is pivoting different from quitting?
Can you think of a real business that changed what they sell?

description.en: Partnership Agreement: Who Does What?
description.es: Partnership Agreement: Who Does What?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Simple partnership template worksheet (printed or written on board)

steps.title: Partnership Introduction
steps.description: Discuss partnerships: two or more people working together in business. Explain benefits (share work, share ideas) and challenges (must agree, share decisions). Introduce partnership agreement activity.

steps.title: Partnership Formation
steps.description: Students pair up to form business partnerships. Discuss together: What business will we run? What will each partner do? Decide on roles: Who handles money? Who creates product? Who talks to customers? Make initial agreements.

steps.title: Partnership Agreement Creation
steps.description: Partners create simple written agreement: business name, what each person will do (responsibilities), how to make decisions (vote? take turns? discuss?), how to split work fairly. Both partners sign agreement.

steps.title: Agreement Sharing & Reflection
steps.description: Pairs share their partnership agreements with another pair or whole class. Explain: How did you divide responsibilities? Why? Discuss: What makes a good partnership? What could go wrong? How does agreement help? Why is it important to decide these things before starting?

discussionQuestions: What business did you and your partner create?
What job will each person do?
Why did you decide to split the money that way?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Negotiated Partnership Agreement with "What If" Clauses
materials: Partnership agreement template with sections for roles, profit split, and problems

steps.title: Partnership Concepts & Examples
steps.description: Discuss business partnerships: examples from real world, why people partner up, potential benefits and challenges. Review what makes partnerships succeed or fail. Introduce partnership agreement project.

steps.title: Finding Compatible Partners
steps.description: Students form pairs based on complementary skills or interests. Partners interview each other: What are your strengths? What do you like doing? What business could we run together? Brainstorm business ideas. Choose one business concept both partners agree on.

steps.title: Responsibility Negotiation
steps.description: Partners discuss and negotiate responsibilities: Who will handle which tasks? How to divide the work fairly? What if someone doesn't do their part? How to make big decisions together? Practice compromise and clear communication.

steps.title: Detailed Agreement Writing
steps.description: Partners create comprehensive written partnership agreement: business description, each partner's specific responsibilities, decision-making process, work schedule, how to handle disagreements, exit plan if partnership doesn't work. Both sign and date.

steps.title: Agreement Presentations
steps.description: Partner pairs present their agreements to class. Explain their business and how they'll work together. Answer questions from classmates. Reflect on partnership planning process.

discussionQuestions: How did you decide who does which job?
Was it easy or hard to agree on how to split the money?
What happens if one partner does all the work but the other partner wants half the money?
Why is it important to have a written agreement?
What did Benny do in the story when he thought 40¢ was too much?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Partnership Contract with Negotiation & Legal Review
materials: Colored pencils or pens for signing
Sample real-world partnership agreements (simplified for kids)

steps.title: Partnership Deep Dive
steps.description: Explore business partnerships in depth: legal structures, real partnership agreements, famous successful and failed partnerships. Discuss equity (who owns what percentage), profit sharing, and legal responsibilities. Set ambitious partnership project goals.

steps.title: Strategic Partner Matching
steps.description: Students complete skills inventory and business interest survey. Use results to find strategically compatible partners: matching skills to business needs. Partners conduct formal business discussion: visions for business, commitment level, long-term goals. Negotiate and form partnerships based on strategic fit.

steps.title: Business Model Development
steps.description: Partners collaboratively develop detailed business model: What will we sell/provide? Who are customers? How will we produce it? What are costs? How will we make profit? Create business model diagram showing all components and how they connect.

steps.title: Comprehensive Agreement Drafting
steps.description: Partners create detailed partnership agreement covering: ownership percentage, capital contributions (what each brings to business), specific role definitions, daily responsibilities, decision-making protocols, conflict resolution process, financial arrangements, performance expectations, exit strategies.

steps.title: Partnership Contract Review
steps.description: Partners exchange agreements with another pair for peer review. Check: Is everything clear? Are responsibilities balanced? Is conflict resolution specified? Provide feedback. Revise agreements based on input.

steps.title: Contract Finalization & Reflection
steps.description: Partners finalize and sign their partnership agreements. Discuss: What surprised you about creating an agreement? What might be hard in real partnerships? Why do written agreements matter? How does your partnership agreement protect both partners?

discussionQuestions: What negotiation strategies worked best for reaching agreement?
Did any partnership split money unevenly? Why was that fair?
What's the difference between a fair split and an equal split?
Why do real businesses write contracts instead of just making promises?
What clause in your agreement do you think will be most important?
In the story, what would have happened if Ellen and the friends DIDN'T write everything down?
extensionIdeas: Compare to real-world business partnerships (research famous business partnerships)
Create a class "Partnership Law Firm" that reviews all agreements for fairness
Role-play dispute scenarios and use the agreements to resolve them
Calculate actual profit splits with sample revenue numbers
Research consignment vs. other partnership types (joint venture, LLC, etc.)

description.en: Holiday Rush: Inventory & Demand Forecasting
description.es: Holiday Rush: Inventory & Demand Forecasting

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 20 craft items (pom-poms, beads, or paper squares) representing "products"

steps.title: Game Setup
steps.description: Students become store owners. Teacher announces: 'It's almost winter holiday!' Students must predict demand and 'buy' inventory. Each student gets 10 tickets to spend on products (pencils, erasers, bookmarks).

steps.title: Inventory Purchase Round
steps.description: Students decide how many of each item to stock. Write predictions on paper. Teacher collects ticket 'payment' for their inventory. Students can't change once purchased.

steps.title: Reveal Customer Demand
steps.description: Teacher reveals: 'Customers want bookmarks for holiday gifts!' Roll die or draw card to show demand: 8 bookmark customers, 1 pencil customer, 0 eraser customers. Students compare to their inventory.

steps.title: Calculate Results & Discussion
steps.description: Students calculate: How many items did you sell? How many left over? Did you run out? Discuss: What happens if you over-order? Under-order? What clues could help predict demand?

discussionQuestions: Was it easy or hard to guess how many people would want?
What happens if you make too many?
Why should you save money from busy weeks?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Order form" cards (15-20 cards with customer orders)

steps.title: Scenario Setup
steps.description: You're a store manager before the holidays. Show product cards with varying demand levels. Introduce the problem: you must order products NOW for customers who will shop LATER. Order too much = waste money. Order too little = miss sales.

steps.title: Prediction Round
steps.description: Students review last year's sales data (simplified cards) and make ordering decisions for 5-6 products. Write predictions: how many of each item will sell this holiday season?

steps.title: Holiday Shopping Simulation
steps.description: Reveal actual demand (draw customer cards). Students check if they had enough inventory. Calculate: items sold, items left over (wasted money), customers turned away (lost sales).

steps.title: Profit Calculation
steps.description: Calculate profit: revenue from sales minus cost of all inventory ordered (including unsold items). Compare results across the class. Who was the best store manager? What strategy did they use?

steps.title: Discussion & Reflection
steps.description: Why is predicting hard? What clues help stores prepare? (Weather, trends, past data.) How do real stores handle leftover holiday inventory? (Sales, clearance, donations.)

discussionQuestions: Which week was hardest to predict? Why?
Did anyone run out of inventory? How did that feel?
Did anyone make too many and have leftovers? What's the cost of that?
Why do businesses save money during busy seasons?
How could you use last year's data to predict this year better?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Retail Simulation with Forecasting, Batch Production & Cash Flow

steps.title: Retail Manager Introduction
steps.description: Introduce the retail challenge: managing a store through three seasons (back-to-school, holiday, summer). Each season has different demand patterns. Show historical sales data charts.

steps.title: Season 1: Back-to-School Ordering
steps.description: Review last year's back-to-school data. Teams decide how much of each product to order. Consider: What do students need in September? How much should you stock?

steps.title: Season 1 Results & Adjustment
steps.description: Reveal actual sales. Calculate profit/loss. What did you learn? Teams adjust strategy for the next round based on results.

steps.title: Season 2: Holiday Rush
steps.description: Holiday demand is highest but hardest to predict. Teams make ordering decisions with higher stakes. Introduce bulk discount option: order more at lower cost per item, but risk more waste.

steps.title: Season 3: Summer Slowdown
steps.description: Demand drops. Teams must decide: order less (safe), or stock sale items to attract bargain hunters? Introduce clearance pricing for leftover holiday inventory.

steps.title: Full-Year Financial Report
steps.description: Calculate total yearly profit across all three seasons. Create a simple bar chart showing revenue, costs, and profit by season. Compare across teams. Crown the best retail manager.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.description: Discuss: Which season was hardest to predict? What would you do differently next year? How do real stores use data to make these decisions? Write one forecasting tip you learned.

discussionQuestions: How accurate were your predictions compared to actual demand?
What strategy worked best: ordering all supplies upfront, or weekly?
When did batch production help the most?
What was the cost of having leftover inventory? What was the cost of running out?
Why does saving 30% during busy season make business sense?
How could you use this year's data to plan for next year?
What real businesses face seasonal rushes like this?" (Toy stores at Christmas, ice cream shops in summer, ski resorts in winter)
extensionIdeas: Graph revenue across all 4 weeks to visualize the seasonal curve
Calculate "opportunity cost" of missed sales when inventory ran out
Research real retail businesses and their seasonal patterns
Create a "Year 2 Plan" incorporating lessons learned from Year 1
Explore "just-in-time inventory" vs. "bulk ordering" trade-offs
Calculate break-even point and profit margins

title.en: Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do?
title.es: Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do?

description.en: Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do?
description.es: Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Index cards or small paper (1 per student)

steps.title: Slow Season Introduction
steps.description: Discuss business seasons: busy times (holidays, summer) and slow times (after holidays, bad weather). Ask: What do businesses do when customers don't come? Introduce slow season strategy challenge.

steps.title: Slow Season Scenario
steps.description: Present scenario: classroom business had busy fall but now it's winter break and sales dropped. Students brainstorm strategies: What could business do? Lower prices? New products? Save money? Advertise? Work on improvements? List all ideas on board.

steps.title: Strategy Selection & Planning
steps.description: Students choose their top 3 strategies from brainstorm. For each, explain: How would this help? What would it cost? When would you do it? Rank strategies: best to worst.

steps.title: Strategy Presentation & Discussion
steps.description: Students share their slow season strategies. Discuss: Which strategies cost money vs. save money? Which are short-term vs. long-term? What do real businesses do in slow seasons? Why is it important to plan for slow times when business is busy?

discussionQuestions: Is slow season bad or just different?
What's one thing you can do when you have extra time?
Should you give up when business is slow? Why not?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Slow Season Strategy Planner" worksheets (template with 4 sections)
Optional: example pictures of businesses in slow vs. busy seasons

steps.title: Seasonal Business Patterns
steps.description: Discuss how businesses experience seasonal changes: ice cream sells more in summer, hot chocolate in winter, school supplies in fall. Graph simple seasonal business pattern on board. Explain slow season challenges and opportunities.

steps.title: Extended Slow Season Simulation
steps.description: Students run classroom business through simulated seasons: busy period (many customers, high sales), then sudden slow period (few customers). Track sales data. Experience the problem firsthand: What happens to money? To inventory? To workers? How does it feel when business is slow?

steps.title: Strategy Research & Development
steps.description: In groups, students research different slow season strategies: cutting costs, introducing new products, saving during busy times, finding new customers, improving business during downtime. Each group becomes expert on one strategy.

steps.title: Strategy Comparison & Planning
steps.description: Groups present their strategies to class. Compare approaches: Which costs money? Which saves money? Which is risky? Which is safe? Students individually choose which strategies they'd use and create simple slow season survival plan.

steps.title: Reflection on Business Cycles
steps.description: Discuss: Why do all businesses have busy and slow times? How can planning ahead help? What's the connection between slow seasons and savings? Why might slow season be good time for improvements?

discussionQuestions: Why do some businesses have slow seasons?
Is it smart to give up during slow times? What should you do instead?
How does saving money during good times help during slow times?
What did Frances's garden teach the team about slow seasons?
How did being nice to Mrs. Torres help the team in January?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: "Business Scenario" cards (6-8 different slow season scenarios)
Research materials (printed examples of real businesses' slow season strategies)
Chart paper and markers for presentations

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do? activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity
steps.description: Students complete the core Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do? activity. Monitor progress, provide support as needed, and ensure students stay on task. Encourage student engagement and participation.

steps.title: Individual Brainstorm
steps.description: Each student writes or draws ONE thing they could do during slow season (practice making lemonade, design new signs, learn new flavors, save money, find new customers).

steps.title: Share & Sort
steps.description: Students share ideas. Teacher writes them on board in categories: PREPARE (get ready for busy time), IMPROVE (make business better), LEARN (get better at skills), CONNECT (talk to customers).

steps.title: Best Idea Vote
steps.description: Class votes on which strategy they think would help most.

steps.title: Connection
steps.description: "In the story, what did the team do during slow January? Ellis built a workbench, Riley made inventory, Layla bought packaging. They PREPARED for spring!"

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between a failing business and a business in slow season?
Why is giving up during slow season a bad idea?
How can slow times actually be GOOD for a business?
What does 'the roots are growing underground' mean for business?" (Frances's garden metaphor)
Why did Ms. Rivera call? How did something the team did in November help them in January?" (relationship building)
What's an emergency fund and why do businesses need one?
Can you think of businesses in our community that have slow seasons? What do they do?
How is 'slow season' different from 'no one wants your product'?
extensionIdeas: Research actual businesses in your community and interview owners about their slow seasons
Track a year-long calendar of business cycles (when are different businesses busy/slow)
Create a "Slow Season Survival Guide" booklet for young entrepreneurs
Calculate: if you make $200 in December and $20 in January, how much should you save from December to survive January?
Compare to personal finances: "Sometimes your family has busy expensive months (back to school, holidays) and quiet months. Why might families save during good months?"

description.en: Business Expo & Season Reflection
description.es: Business Expo & Season Reflection

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

steps.title: Business Expo Introduction
steps.description: Explain Business Expo: students will showcase classroom businesses, products made, or business ideas from the season. Set up expo format: booth displays, presentations, visitor time. Review expectations.

steps.title: Expo Booth Setup
steps.description: Students create expo booths: display products or business materials, make signs with business names, create simple presentations about what they learned. Organize workspace to show business concept clearly.

steps.title: Expo Presentations
steps.description: Students practice quick business presentations: What's your business? What did you learn? What was challenging? What are you proud of? Keep it brief (30-60 seconds).

steps.title: Business Expo Event
steps.description: Run the expo! Half the class presents at booths while half visits. Then switch roles. Presenters explain their businesses, visitors ask questions and learn about different business concepts. Celebrate student work.

steps.title: Season Reflection
steps.description: Gather as class. Reflect on full business season: What was most important thing you learned about business? About money? About working with others? How will you use what you learned? What surprised you most?

discussionQuestions: What was the most fun activity we did this season?
What was the hardest lesson to learn?
Would you want to run a real business someday?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Mini Business Expo with Reflection Posters
materials: Large paper (1 per student or small group)
Reflection prompts printed or written on board

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the Business Expo & Season Reflection activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity
steps.description: Students complete the core Business Expo & Season Reflection activity. Monitor progress, provide support as needed, and ensure students stay on task. Encourage student engagement and participation.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.description: "In the story, the friends looked back at everything they learned. Not just money — but how they grew as people. What did YOU learn this season?"

steps.title: Individual Reflection
steps.description: Each student draws or writes ONE business lesson on their card. "The most important thing I learned about business is..."

steps.title: Share Circle
steps.description: Students sit in circle. Each shares their lesson. Teacher writes themes on chart paper.

steps.title: Class Summary
steps.description: "Look at everything we learned together! Which lesson shows up the most?"

discussionQuestions: Which business lesson will you use in real life?
What surprised you about running a business?
If you could do one activity again, which would it be?
How did working with partners help you?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Business Expo with Financial Analysis & Presentations
materials: Large poster board or tri-fold display boards (1 per student/team)

steps.title: Introduction & Setup
steps.description: Introduce the Business Expo & Season Reflection activity. Review materials and instructions. Set clear goals and expectations. Organize students into working groups or positions.

steps.title: Main Activity
steps.description: Students complete the core Business Expo & Season Reflection activity. Monitor progress, provide support as needed, and ensure students stay on task. Encourage student engagement and participation.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.description: "In the story, the friends looked back at everything they learned. Not just money — but how they grew as people. What did YOU learn this season?"

steps.title: Individual Reflection
steps.description: Each student draws or writes ONE business lesson on their card. "The most important thing I learned about business is..."

steps.title: Share Circle
steps.description: Students sit in circle. Each shares their lesson. Teacher writes themes on chart paper.

steps.title: Class Summary
steps.description: "Look at everything we learned together! Which lesson shows up the most?"

discussionQuestions: **Financial Analysis:** "Which business made the most profit? Why do you think that happened?
**Product Performance:** "If you could only sell ONE product, which would you choose and why?
**Strategic Thinking:** "The friends in the story chose Option B — stay the same size. Would you make the same choice? Why or why not?
**Personal Growth:** "How did you grow as a person, not just as a business owner?
**Partnership Reflection:** "What made a good business partner? How did you handle disagreements?
**Future Planning:** "If you ran your business for another six months, what would you change?
extensionIdeas: Invite parents/families to attend expo as "investors"
Create video presentations of business journeys
Write reflective essays: "My Season as an Entrepreneur"
Develop actual year-long plan similar to friends in story (Spring/Summer/Fall/Winter goals)
Research real young entrepreneurs and their stories
Create "Business Advice" book for next year's students
